activity: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
knowledge_domain: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
fact: In the United States and many other countries, a play is protected by copyright automatically as soon as it is written down, without needing to be registered.
story:
The auditorium smelled of dust and radiator paint, and Mason had claimed the third row of flip-up seats as his office because the folding tables were all taken by louder people. The showcase was Friday. It was currently Tuesday, which meant his ten-minute play about the summer his father moved out existed so far as three lines of dialogue and a stage direction that said only, "A porch. Evening." Across the aisle, Ryan sat with his script turned face down every time anyone walked past, which in a room of twenty people meant he spent most of the hour hunched over like a man guarding his lunch.

"What are you hiding," Mason said, not really asking.

"You'll steal it." Ryan said it flatly, the way he prognosticated most things, with total confidence and no evidence. "Izak already pitched a play about a guy whose dad leaves. That's my territory."

"My play is about my dad," Mason said. "I can't steal my own dad."

"You don't get how this works. We show Friday, then everybody goes to drama camp in July with the same material, and somebody faster rewrites it and shops it around and suddenly it's theirs." Ryan tapped the back of his script. "I'm not handing mine to anyone until the last minute."

Izak, who had heard his name from four rows away, came over the way he did everything, sideways and grinning. He was writing about his grandmother's kitchen, he said, and he wasn't going to let Ryan's paranoia ruin the week, because the whole point of the showcase was that Mr. Le had asked for a moment from their actual lives, and your actual life was the one thing nobody could take. Mason thought about that on the walk home. Izak's position was generous and, Mason suspected, slightly wrong. Ryan's position was mean and, Mason also suspected, slightly right. He liked not having to choose yet.

At home he typed the whole fact of the matter into the search bar, the way you do when an argument is bothering you more than the homework is: does someone own a play when they write it. The answer came back faster than he expected, and it was plainer than either Ryan's barricade or Izak's open hands. In the United States and a lot of other countries, a play is protected by copyright automatically as soon as it's written down. You don't have to register it. Mason read the sentence twice, then a third time, feeling something settle and something else loosen. Ryan had been guarding a locked door. At the same time, the protection attached to the words on the page, and Izak's "your life" theory suddenly looked shakier, because a version of your life in somebody else's sentences belonged to them. Mason sat with that for a while, then opened a new document and started writing the porch scene for real.

Wednesday he wrote nine pages. Thursday he cut two of them, which hurt more than writing them had. Mr. Le moved through the rows during rehearsal like a man taking inventory, pausing at Mason's seat long enough to read a page over his shoulder. "You let the silence carry the end," he said. "Brave choice for a first play." That was all. Mason had hoped for more, then realized the restraint was the compliment.

He found Ryan in the wings Thursday afternoon, still hoarding. He could have said told you and enjoyed it. Instead he sat on an auxiliary lighting case that somebody had dragged behind the curtain, and told Ryan what he'd found, laying it out the way it had come to him: it's yours the second you write it down, here and in a bunch of other countries, no registration, nothing. Ryan's shoulders came down maybe an inch. "So Izak can't just rewrite my dad thing."

"He can write his own dad thing. He can't take yours." Mason shrugged. "Honestly I still don't know if that makes the paranoia pointless or if you were right to be careful and just wrong about the mechanism. Both feel true."

"That's the most annoying sentence you've ever said," Ryan said, but he turned his script right side up.

Friday the auditorium filled with parents and the smell of somebody's microwave popcorn, against all rules. Izak went second and was wonderful, and Mason watched his own genealogy of the past year, the porch, the father, the unsaid thing, stand up in two actors he'd met on Monday, and it was stranger and better than he had imagined, and it was over in ten minutes, and it was his either way. Afterward Ryan found him by the exit doors holding his script, which now had coffee rings on it and a torn corner from being passed around.

"Read it," Ryan said, holding it out flat, like an offering, or a dare. "Tell me if the ending works."

activity: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
knowledge_domain: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
fact: Under the 2017 American guideline, elevated blood pressure means a systolic reading of 120 to 129 with a diastolic reading below 80.
story:
The printout went up on the bathroom mirror on Tuesday, held by a strip of tape that had already lost half its stick. Her mother had stopped at the pharmacy machine on the way home from work, sat with her arm in the cuff while the machine hissed and squeezed, and come away with a slip of paper that said 125 over 78. She'd taped it beside the dental floss so she would see it every morning, and then she'd gone to look up a recipe for something with lentils in it. Kaylee stood in front of it now with her toothbrush in one hand, reading the little numbers like they were a message in a language she hadn't taken yet.

She was supposed to be learning this anyway. Ms. Ross had assigned the health unit project the day before: learn to interpret a blood pressure reading, and be able to explain, out loud, how diet and exercise change it. Kaylee had assumed she'd invent a patient, some tidy fictional person with a tidy fictional history. Now the assignment had climbed off the page and taped itself to her own mirror.

She texted Remy from the bathroom floor, back against the tub. Remy was the one who read the fine print on everything, who had once spent a weekend on the Federal Reserve's website for fun.

"Systolic over diastolic," Remy wrote back almost immediately. "Top number, bottom number. That part's easy. The part where it gets weird is the categories."

Kaylee pulled up the guideline on her phone, the 2017 American one, and sat with it. The categories were laid out like steps. She ran her finger under the words, then looked up at the mirror, then back down. One hundred twenty-five. The top number sat inside a band from 120 to 129, and the bottom number, 78, was below 80. There was a name printed on that step. "It's elevated," she said out loud, to the toothbrush, to the printout, to nobody. "One twenty-five over seventy-eight is elevated."

Her mother's voice came through the door. "Are you talking to yourself in there?"

"Talking to your blood pressure."

"Is it bad?"

Kaylee looked at the guideline again. There were steps above that one, higher numbers with harder names, and steps below it, a category called normal that started under 120. Her mother's reading was not on the top step. It was not on the bottom step either. It was on the one in between, the one whose name Kaylee now knew how to say. "It's elevated," she called back. "Not the bad one. Not normal either. There's a middle."

There was a silence on the other side of the door, the kind where someone is deciding how frightened to be. "Middle is fine," her mother said finally. "Middle I can work with."

That night Kaylee sat on the closed toilet lid with her notes while her mother ran the shower, and tried to build the second half of the project, the part about how diet and exercise change a reading. This was where the thinking got divided against itself. Marvin's position, argued loudly in the cafeteria on Wednesday, was that if a number was only "middle," then changing your whole life over it was an overreaction, and people who did that were treating a drizzle like a hurricane. Remy's position, delivered with the mild stubbornness Remy brought to everything, was that a middle number was exactly the moment to act, because once you were on the top step the whole business stopped being yours to manage so easily. Kaylee had taken Marvin's side that day mostly because Marvin had been so bellicose about it, all raised voice and slapped table, and something in her wanted to calm the room down rather than pile on.

Now, alone, she turned both positions over. Marvin wasn't wrong that panic was useless; her mother panicking would mean takeout and stress and no walks. But Remy wasn't wrong that "elevated" was a signal, and a signal you could still answer. Kaylee's own considered position, the one she would say to Ms. Ross and mean, was that the middle category mattered precisely because it hadn't yet become anything worse, and that the right response to it wasn't fear, it was lentils, and walking, and a follow-up reading in a few weeks to see if anything had moved. She also had to be honest, in her write-up, about what she couldn't claim: she did not know, from one number on one evening, whether her mother's reading would drift up, drift down, or sit exactly where it was. A single data point was a denouement with no story before it. She would say that too, because Ms. Ross gave better marks for admitted uncertainty than for invented certainty, and because it was true.

Saturday morning her mother knocked on the bathroom door while Kaylee was brushing her hair. "I made the lentil thing," she said through the door. "It needs salt. Also, there's a machine at the pharmacy by the nail polish aisle, and I thought next Saturday, before groceries, we'd do it again. Both of us this time. You can practice your project on me."

Kaylee opened the door, toothbrush still in hand. "You'd be my real patient, then. Not the fake one I made up."

"Is the fake one more cooperative?"

"Much. He does everything I tell him." Kaylee pointed the toothbrush at the printout on the mirror. "Same time of day matters, though. That's in my notes. Evening numbers and morning numbers can't just be compared like they're the same thing, and I'm not going to pretend they can."

Her mother looked at the slip of paper for a long moment, the way she looked at crossword clues she almost had. "Okay," she said. "Saturday morning, then. You bring the notes." She reached past Kaylee and pressed the corner of the tape down flat with her thumb, fixing the part that had been curling up all week.

activity: the idea that historians disagree about the past because sources are partial and questions change
knowledge_domain: the idea that historians disagree about the past because sources are partial and questions change
fact: In 1824 German historian Leopold von Ranke wrote that his work aimed only to show the past 'as it actually was', rather than to judge it or instruct the present.
story:
Addison spread her books across her grandfather's kitchen table because the table was the only surface in the house big enough, and because her grandfather wanted her where he could see her. The essay question sat at the top of her notebook in Ms. Haddad's tidy print: Can the past be described without taking a side? She had been circling the question for two days and had produced a page of notes that contradicted each other, which was, she suspected, the point.

"You're writing about truth," her grandfather said, setting down a mug of tea she hadn't asked for. "Good. Most people write about opinions and call it truth."

"That's not helpful," Addison said.

"Nothing is, at the start."

The house was spartan since her grandmother had died in March, the chairs pushed to the walls, the shelves half-empty because her uncle had taken boxes away in June. What remained was her grandfather's filing cabinet, four drawers of letters and photographs and newspaper clippings, and Addison had come for the weekend partly to write her essay and partly, though she hadn't said so, to be near that cabinet. She had a smaller, quieter reason too: the folder marked 1989.

Her phone buzzed against the table. Linkin, from the class group chat: did you find a source for the Ranke thing yet? Ms. Haddad wants the quote exact. Addison typed back that she had it, and she did, copied into her notebook from the textbook: in 1824 the German historian Leopold von Ranke wrote that his work aimed only to show the past "as it actually was", rather than to judge it or instruct the present. Jason had read the sentence aloud in class and then asked whether that was even possible, and Ms. Haddad had said only, that's your essay question, isn't it, and moved on.

Addison opened her notebook to that page. Ranke's sentence looked simple, and it was not. She remembered standing in Ms. Haddad's classroom the day before, the window open, Jason arguing that every historian picked a beginning and an ending and that picking was already a side. Addison had defended Ranke then, or had wanted to: if you just showed what happened, in order, without decoration, surely anyone could see it the same way. Jason had shrugged. Sure, he said, and then asked who tells you what happened.

That was the question she couldn't shake, and it was why she was at the filing cabinet by four o'clock, kneeling on the wooden floor, pulling the 1989 folder into her lap. Her grandfather had worked at the plant for thirty-one years and had left in 1989, and the story she'd grown up on was that he'd quit on principle, that he'd refused to sign something, that the management had wanted to make an example and he'd made himself one first. Her grandmother used to call him the family's dissident, half joking, the way she said it about people in books. Her grandfather liked the word. He'd used it about himself at Thanksgiving, at funerals, once to a cashier who hadn't asked.

The folder held something else. There was a letter, typed on plant stationery, dated that spring, offering him a transfer to a branch office, a smaller role but a role, signed by a director whose name Addison didn't know. There was a second letter, his own draft of a refusal, and then a clipping from the local paper about layoffs at the plant that autumn, two hundred positions, and a handwritten list on the back of an envelope of names she recognized from her grandmother's stories, people who had stayed and people who hadn't.

"You went through my files," her grandfather said from the doorway. He didn't move from it.

"You told me I could. Last summer. You said, anything in there is yours."

"I said that about the photographs."

"The papers too. Nana heard you say it."

He crossed the room and took the first letter from her hand, held it the way he held things he was deciding about. "They offered me a demotion," he said. "That's what a transfer was, there."

"The paper says layoffs in October. You left in May."

"The two things are not connected."

"They might be."

He set the letter on the cabinet, face down, and she watched him not look at it. "You want to write your essay about me?"

"I want to know what happened."

"Which thing. The letter, or the paper, or what your grandmother told you at dinner." He sat down on the floor across from her, his knees cracking, and it was the closest they had sat since the funeral. "She was there. She read this letter before I answered it. She'd tell it differently than I do, and she was in the room."

"Then there's no version that's just what happened."

"There's everything that happened," he said. "There's no version of it that fits in a sentence."

They sat with the folder between them. Addison picked up the refusal draft, his handwriting younger and harder than it was now, and read the opening line, which thanked the director and said the position could not be accepted, and gave no reason at all. The letter exculpated nobody, herself least of all; it only stood there, partial, refusing to explain itself even in its own words.

She photographed the letter, then the clipping, then the envelope with the names, and texted one to Linkin without commentary. Ranke again, she thought, underlining the sentence in her notebook, twice. Only to show the past "as it actually was". She underlined it and then, beside it, wrote: but which parts are the past, and who decided.

Her grandfather pulled a second envelope from the back of the folder, one she hadn't reached yet. "There's more in here you haven't seen," he said. "You'd better decide whether you want it before you ask."

"I want it," Addison said, and put out her hand.

activity: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
knowledge_domain: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
fact: In Mahanoy Area School District v. B.L. (2021), the Supreme Court ruled 8-1 that a school violated a student's free speech by punishing an off-campus Snapchat post.
story:
The courthouse smelled like floor wax and old paper, and Nicholas stood at the metal detector with his backpack open while a guard waved a wand along the seams. In his notebook, held shut with a rubber band, were forty pages of notes on a case called Mahanoy Area School District v. B.L., which he had chosen that morning and now half regretted. Ms. Brennan had assigned each of them a Supreme Court case to argue before a panel of seniors in the ceremonial courtroom on the third floor, and she had made it harder than it needed to be: each of them had to argue both sides.

He found Celine near the water fountain, flipping through index cards with the fixed calm of someone who had practiced in front of a mirror. "What did you get?" she asked. "Tinker," Nicholas said. "No, wait. Mahanoy." He watched her expression go sympathetic, the way people look at someone who has drawn the hard question at a debate. "The Snapchat one," she said. "That's all anybody's going to care about."

The case was simple to state and impossible to hold still. A student, off campus, on a weekend, had posted something crude on Snapchat about her school and her team, and the school had suspended her from cheerleading for it. The Supreme Court had ruled eight to one that the school violated her free speech by punishing that off-campus post. Nicholas had read the opinion twice on the bus, and then a third time at his kitchen table while his mother asked him, from the stove, whether he understood that people lost jobs over less. He had said he understood, which was not the same as saying it was true.

The courtroom itself was smaller than he had pictured, oak and dark green carpet, a judge's bench tall enough that the seniors sitting behind it had to lean forward to seem attentive. Malia was already there, third row, with her phone flat on her knee like a device for recording weather. She caught his eye and mouthed, which side first, and Nicholas held up two fingers, meaning the school, meaning he would have to argue that the punishment was right before he argued that it was wrong.

When his name was called, the floor changed under his feet, softer, and his voice came out lower than he expected. He argued for the school first. He talked about order, about the biome of a school, the way every part of it depended on the others, how a team was not a public square and a coach was not the government. A senior with glasses asked him whether a Snapchat post made off campus was really the school's to govern, and Nicholas said, with the confidence of a borrowed coat, that the effects flowed back through the doors on Monday morning. It sounded thinner the moment he said it.

Then he sat down for two minutes, and something in him coagulated, the scattered nerves settling into something with a shape, and when he stood again he argued the other side. He told the panel that the Supreme Court had ruled eight to one that the school violated the student's free speech by punishing an off-campus post, that even the lone dissenter had not defended the suspension itself, and that a rule allowing schools to reach into weekends would have no edge to it. Celine, from the fountain bench, gave him a small nod, the kind you give someone who has finally stopped performing.

Afterward, in the crepuscular light coming through the tall west windows, the seniors conferred in whispers. Ms. Brennan found him by the railing that divided the well of the court from the seats. "Which side do you actually believe?" she asked, and Nicholas looked at the carpet for a moment. "The student should have won," he said. "But I don't know where the line is, exactly. I argued like I knew, both times." Ms. Brennan seemed about to answer, then wrote something in her folder instead.

The seniors came back with their verdict, a narrow win on one side, and Nicholas could not tell from their faces which, and found that he did not lean forward to find out. Malia held up her phone and showed him the screen, the actual opinion, the paragraph he had underlined on the bus. "Eight to one," she said. "You had it right." He looked at it a second time anyway, the way you check a lock, and then slid the rubber band back over his notebook.

activity: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
knowledge_domain: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
fact: The First Amendment limits what the government can do to speech; it does not by itself stop a private employer or private company from restricting speech.
story:
The courthouse smelled of floor wax and old paper, and Sophia kept her legal pad balanced on her knee so the bailiff would not think she was nervous, though she was. Mr. Diallo had arranged for the mock court to sit in a real courtroom, a favor from a cousin who clerked there, and the wooden benches had actual initials carved into them, which made the whole thing feel less like a class exercise and more like something that could follow her around.

She had drawn Tinker v. Des Moines plus a modern twist the coach had invented, and she was expected to argue both sides, petitioner and respondent, ten minutes each. The twist was this: a fictional student, suspended not by a school but by a private debate platform, claimed her free speech rights had been violated when the platform removed her posts. Sophia's plan had been simple all week. Side one, speech deserves protection. Side two, schools may regulate disruption. She had a folder full of index cards to prove it.

Mohamad slid into the bench beside her, straightening his tie with the smugness of someone holding a folded piece of paper. "I'm the justice who gets to ask questions," he said. "Susan told me to look up something before you go."

"Susan told you to sabotage me?"

"Susan told me to check whether your second side is even legal." He unfolded the paper, a printout with a highlighted paragraph, and held it where only she could see it. "The First Amendment limits what the government can do to speech," he read, quietly but clearly. "It doesn't by itself stop a private employer or a private company from restricting speech."

Sophia stared at the highlighted lines. All week she had built her respondent argument on the idea that the platform, like a school, could punish disruptive speech, and she had framed it as a limit on the student's First Amendment rights, a balancing test, a scale. But the platform wasn't the government at all. There was nothing to balance. Her whole second side had been arguing about a protection that never applied, like litigating a fence line on land nobody owned.

"That can't be right," she said, though even as she said it she recognized the sound of someone defending a position because she had already written it down.

"Ask her, then," Mohamad said, nodding toward Susan, who was sitting in the front row with the actual case file open on her lap.

Sophia walked down the center aisle while the other team set up, and dropped into the seat beside Susan. "Did you know my second argument was wrong the whole time?"

"I thought it might be," Susan said, not looking up. "You kept saying the platform violated her rights, and Mohamad said that sounded off, so we checked. I was going to tell you Tuesday, but you were so confident. I figured you'd find it." She turned a page. "Also I wanted to see what you'd do."

"That's a terrible reason."

"It's a very good reason. You're about to stand up in a courtroom and argue both sides of something. If you can't survive finding out you're wrong on a Tuesday, the courtroom's going to be a rough forty minutes."

The bailiff called the session to order, and the mock justices filed in, Mohamad last, taking his seat with the composure of a person who had practiced it in a mirror. Sophia stood for her first argument, the petitioner's side, and it went the way prepared things go, smooth and a little hollow, her cards in order, her voice steady. The black armbands, the Vietnam protest, the students who wore them and won. She sat down almost enjoying herself.

Then it was time to switch sides, and she left her index cards on the bench.

"Your respondent claims the platform infringed the student's constitutional rights," Mohamad said, leaning into his microphone. "Walk us through that."

She had two roads in front of her, and she could see both of them clearly. She could read her prepared cards, make the balancing argument she no longer believed, and probably win on polish. Or she could say the true thing and build the second side from the ground up, that the First Amendment limits what the government can do to speech, that it does not by itself stop a private employer or a private company from restricting speech, and that if the student wanted protection from the platform, she would have to find it somewhere other than the amendment Sophia had been waving around all week.

"The First Amendment limits what the government can do to speech," she said. "It does not by itself stop a private company from restricting speech. My prepared argument was wrong about that, and I'd rather lose honestly than win on it."

The courtroom went quiet in the way rooms do when someone abandons a script. Mohamad was the first to smile. Somewhere behind her, she heard Susan say, quietly, "There it is," and one of the other justices, a senior named to the panel for his gravitas, whispered to his neighbor that the whole amendment framework was antiquated anyway, built for a world of town squares. Sophia didn't know yet whether that was true or whether it was the next thing she'd have to check.

"Then argue it from where it actually stands," Mohamad said. "You have eight minutes."

activity: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
knowledge_domain: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
fact: Chlamydia and gonorrhea often cause no symptoms, so testing is the only reliable way for a person to know whether they have one.
story:
Sarah sat at the kitchen table with the clinic pamphlets fanned out in front of her like a losing hand of cards, and her mother's voice carried down the hall through the interminable phone call about the neighbors' fence, which meant she had at least twenty minutes before anyone asked what she was reading. She was supposed to be the peer health presenter on Friday, twelve minutes in front of the junior health classes, and Mr. O'Brien had said, in his dry way, "You'll know it when you can explain it to someone who doesn't want to hear it." That had seemed like a small requirement. It was not.

She had volunteered because Skylar had dared her, more or less, in the parking lot after fourth period. "You're good at talking," Skylar had said, which was the kind of compliment that doubled as a dare, and Sarah had signed her name on the sheet before she could think of a reason not to. Now the reasons crowded in. The packet covered consent, contraception, and testing, and the testing pages kept sliding into clinical language she couldn't hold still in her mouth: asymptomatic, screening, notification of partners. She read a sentence three times and it dissolved each time she looked up at the refrigerator.

Chaya came through the back door without knocking, which was the arrangement between their mothers going back to middle school, and dropped her backpack on a chair. "You're studying on a Wednesday," she said. "Voluntarily." She pulled a pamphlet toward her, the one with the cartoon uterus, and raised an eyebrow. "Is this your thing? The Friday thing?"

"My thing," Sarah confirmed. She watched Chaya read, waiting for the joke. Chaya's wants were usually simple and loud: the last slice of pizza, the window seat, the solo in the spring concert. But lately she had gone quieter, and Sarah had been meaning to ask about that and hadn't.

"Explaining consent to freshmen," Chaya said. "That's brutal. They'll either laugh at everything or sit there like stones." She turned the pamphlet over. "Which one are you worst at?"

"Testing," Sarah said, surprising herself with the honesty. "The rest I can do. Condoms, the pill, the implant, whatever. Consent is actually the easiest because it's just, you know, freely given, reversible, everyone sober enough to know what they're agreeing to. But the clinic stuff, I don't know how to make it real."

Chaya was quiet for a moment, picking at the pamphlet's corner. Then she said, in a voice with a false bottom in it, "Would the clinic just, like, test anyone? Even if nothing's wrong?"

Sarah looked up. The question had come out too carefully, the way Chaya asked for rides when she didn't want to say where she was going. "Even if nothing's wrong," Sarah said slowly, "you could still have something. That's actually the part I keep rereading." She found the page, ran her finger under the line. "Chlamydia and gonorrhea often cause no symptoms at all. So testing is the only reliable way to know whether you have one."

Chaya's face did something complicated. "But if you feel fine," she said, "you'd kind of assume you were fine. That's how people think."

"That's how I would think," Sarah said. "Last week I would have assumed that too." She turned the pamphlet so Chaya could see the whole page, and neither of them said the obvious, which was that the question hadn't been theoretical. The kettle ticked on the stove. Down the hall, her mother laughed at something the fence man had said.

"Skylar said the campus clinic does it for students for free," Chaya said finally. "But I don't even know where it is."

"Skylar went?" Sarah asked, and filed that away as another thing she hadn't known about Skylar, alongside the fact that he apparently knew where the clinic was. Her mind was already assembling Friday's presentation, sentence by sentence, testing it against the person in front of her, which was the only audience that mattered now. "It's on Delancey, by the pharmacy. I can go with you Thursday if you want. I need to visit anyway, for the presentation. Take pictures of the front desk so the freshmen know it's not some dungeon."

"You'd do that?" Chaya asked, and then, recovering herself, "I mean, fine, Thursday," as if she were doing Sarah the favor, and Sarah let her have it, because that was the price and it was a small one.

Her mother finally hung up and came into the kitchen, saw the pamphlets, and did not excoriate her, which Sarah had braced for; instead she just put a hand briefly on Sarah's shoulder on her way to the fridge, which was somehow harder to bear. Sarah thought about telling her, and thought about not telling her about Chaya at all, because it wasn't hers to tell, and that distinction felt like the real test, harder than any presentation. Fear of your mother finding out could be its own disincentive, she thought, a reason people her age never walked through a clinic door at all, and she wrote in the margin of her notes: say this out loud on Friday.

Thursday after school they took the bus, Chaya with her hood up and her earbuds in, Sarah carrying the pamphlets like a shield. The waiting room had beige chairs and a fish tank with one depressed angel fish, and the intake form was on a clipboard, and Chaya filled it out with her knee bouncing the whole time. The nurse who called her back was younger than either of them expected, and when Chaya said, "I feel fine, though, is this even necessary," the nurse just nodded like she heard it fifty times a day and said the test would tell them what feeling fine couldn't.

Sarah sat in the beige chair and took out her notes and crossed out her first paragraph, the one full of statistics, and wrote at the top of a fresh page: start with the part nobody believes. When Chaya came out, she was folding the aftercare sheet into eighths, very small, and she dropped into the chair beside Sarah and didn't say anything for a minute.

"So Friday," Chaya said. "Practice it on me on the bus."

Sarah flipped to the first page. "Okay. Consent first."

"Obviously consent first," Chaya said, and pulled out one earbud to listen.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Around 1420 in Florence, Filippo Brunelleschi demonstrated linear perspective, the technique of drawing lines that meet at a vanishing point to show depth on a flat surface.
story:
The assignment had sounded simple when Mr. Robinson said it: draw the school hallway so it looked like you could walk into it. Eric had thought that would take maybe forty minutes. It had now taken three days, and his hallway looked like a hallway photographed by a camera that had been flattened by a steamroller. The doors sat on the floor. The trophy case floated. The ceiling, if it was a ceiling, appeared to be in front of the lockers, which was a bold architectural statement but not the one he wanted.

"You've drawn a hallway that exists in four dimensions," said Aimee, leaning over his shoulder. "Two of them are time."

"Thank you. It's very modern."

"It's very wrong." She tapped the paper where the lockers marched along in a polite row, each exactly the same size, refusing to shrink no matter how far away they claimed to be. "The far ones should be smaller. Everything should be getting smaller and squishing together and you're not letting it."

Eric knew she was right in the way you know a door is locked, which is to say he kept pushing it anyway. He tried drawing the far lockers shorter, but then they just looked like lockers for a shorter species of student. He erased so hard the paper thinned to a whisper and threatened to expropriate the drawing beneath it, that ghostly first attempt he'd abandoned on Monday. The eraser crumbs accumulated on the table like the debris of a small, defeated civilization.

Sarina slid into the seat across from him with her own drawing, which was infuriatingly good. Her hallway receded into the paper as if the page had a hole in it. "It's called linear perspective," she said, because she could never resist, and she arranged three pencils on the table so they converged on a single point. "Around 1420 in Florence, Filippo Brunelleschi demonstrated it. You draw your lines so they meet at one vanishing point, and boom, depth, on a flat surface."

"You just did my homework for me and I resent it and I'm grateful," Eric said. He lined up his ruler from the corners of his hallway toward a point on the paper and drew. Something happened immediately, and it felt slightly illegal, like he'd found a door where the wall was supposed to be. The ceiling sloped down. The floor sloped up. The lockers, obeying the ruler as if it were a law of nature, shrank into the distance. His flat steamrollered corridor became a corridor.

"Mr. Robinson is going to think you suddenly became talented," Aimee said. "We should manage his expectations."

"Tell him it was the zeitgeist," Eric said. "Renaissance energy flowing through the art room, I merely channeled it."

"You don't know what that word means."

"I know exactly what it means. It means I get credit for forces beyond my control." He was drawing faster now, and a small problem surfaced: the vanishing point worked beautifully for the walls, but the drinking fountain he'd stubbornly included looked like it was melting sideways toward the point, a drinking fountain in the process of being expropriated by geometry itself. He laughed at it, and Aimee laughed at it, and Sarina pretended not to but failed.

He fixed the fountain by deciding, after some staring, that it didn't have to obey the same lines as the walls. Objects had their own angles. He was not sure this was correct. He was, in fact, mostly guessing, and he found he didn't mind; Brunelleschi had demonstrated the big trick, the part with the converging lines and the vanishing point and the sudden depth, and everything after that was Eric figuring out the smaller tricks by ruining them first. There was something almost anachronistic about doing it this way, a boy in 2025 bent over graph paper with a ruler, rediscovering in miniature what a Florentine had worked out six hundred years ago, but the pencil in his hand didn't care about the calendar.

Mr. Robinson drifted past their table on his circuit of the room, paused, and looked at the hallway for a long moment. Eric waited for the verdict, for some pronouncement about technique or composition.

"Fountain's crooked," Mr. Robinson said, and moved on.

"It's in perspective," Eric called after him.

"It's crooked in perspective."

Aimee snorted into her sleeve. Sarina held up her pencil like a tiny torch of vindication. Eric looked at the melting fountain, then at his vanishing point, then picked up his eraser and, very gently, went back in.

activity: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
knowledge_domain: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
fact: Compound or coating chocolate, which replaces some or all cocoa butter with other fats, sets without tempering but does not have the same snap.
story:
The marble slab had belonged to Zoey's grandmother, and before that to nobody her grandmother would name. It was the only thing she had asked for when the house began emptying itself, room by room, into boxes marked with a cousin's handwriting. Zoey set it on the kitchen counter on a morning in late August, a week before she left for college, and took out the chocolate she had bought with her first paycheck from the garden centre.

Her grandmother had tempered chocolate the way other people said their prayers, without ever once explaining what they were doing. Zoey had watched her do it at this counter a hundred times, and now that she was alone with the slab and a double boiler and a thermometer, she understood that watching was not the same as knowing. She melted the chocolate to forty-five degrees, cooled it against the marble with a spatula, worked it back and forth until it thickened and glossed over, then returned it to gentle heat. The first batch bloomed white within an hour, dull as an old coin. The second streaked. She ate the failures in small guilty squares while they still tasted good.

Charlie called on the third morning, from a campsite up north where the reception cut in and out. He was making dipped strawberries, he said, for his little sister's birthday, and he'd bought a bag of candy melts at the supermarket.

"You have to temper those," Zoey said, phone wedged between shoulder and ear while she stirred. "Melt, cool on marble, warm it back up. Otherwise it stays streaky."

"Tempering? Mine just set up hard when I dipped them. I didn't do anything." There was wind on the line, and his sister shouting somewhere behind it. "They're shiny too. Kind of."

"They're compound chocolate," Zoey said, mostly to herself. She had read it on the package in the supermarket aisle, the night she'd stood there for ten minutes choosing. "Coating chocolate. They replace some or all of the cocoa butter with other fats, so they set without tempering. But they don't have the same snap." She heard her own voice deliver it flat and quick, like a card she'd memorized, and she was embarrassed by how much she liked knowing it.

"Huh," Charlie said. "Well, they taste fine. Good luck with your thing." The line dropped before she could tell him that fine was exactly the word, that the whole difference lived inside that word.

Ms. Tan, who had been her grandmother's neighbour for thirty years, came by that afternoon with a box of jars she was returning. She stood in the doorway a long moment, looking at the marble slab, and did not offer to teach Zoey anything, for which Zoey was grateful. "She used to let me scrape the bowl," Ms. Tan said instead. "When my English was bad, and I didn't want to talk, she didn't make me talk. She made me scrape the bowl." She set the jars down and left without any of the florid farewell speeches the other neighbours had given, the ones about memory and legacy that made Zoey's ears hot, and that was the second thing she was grateful for that day.

The fourth batch, that evening, set with a snap. She tested it on the counter, on her teeth, on the back of a cold spoon, and each time it broke clean and bright, with a sound like a small door closing properly. She stood over the slab feeling something she could not decide was triumph or trespass. It was as if she had finally been let into a room by proving she could pick the lock, and now that she was inside she wasn't sure the room was hers.

Her mother came in from packing and took a piece without asking, the way she took everything in that house lately, as though the taking were itself a kind of grief. "You know she never taught anyone that," her mother said. "Not your aunt, not me. She said it was too fussy, that we'd all get impatient and ruin it."

"Maybe she was right," Zoey said. "I ruined it four times."

"You didn't get impatient, though." Her mother said it lightly, but they both heard the other sentence underneath, the one about who had inherited the patience and who had inherited the leaving, and neither of them was willing to touch it. Her mother went back upstairs. Zoey poured the leftover tempered chocolate out onto parchment and spread it thin, because her grandmother always did, and because the alternative was admitting there was no one left to eat it.

She had been thinking, all week, that there were two ways to understand the old woman, and that she had spent most of her life choosing the wrong one. There was the reading where her grandmother was withholding, a keeper of techniques, someone who taught by omission. And there was the reading where the withholding was the teaching, where scraping the bowl for thirty years was the lesson and the tempering was just the excuse. Charlie's candy melts kept coming back to her as she worked. They were easy, they worked for everyone, and they gave you something that set hard and looked fine and never snapped. Maybe her grandmother had refused to be a candy melt. Maybe she had only ever wanted to be difficult on purpose, the way real chocolate is difficult on purpose, so that the thing you got at the end could only be earned. Or maybe that was a story Zoey was telling herself, a hermeneutics of a dead woman, and the truth was smaller and meaner and not worth excavating. She could not decide, and she was old enough now to know that the not deciding was going to last.

The phone buzzed against the counter. A photo from Charlie: nine lopsided strawberries on a paper plate, their coatings dull in the firelight, his sister grinning behind them with chocolate on her teeth. "Best birthday ever," he had written. "Tastes better than it snaps, trust me."

Zoey looked at her own chocolate, laid out in a perfect dark sheet, glossy as a mirror, snapped clean as proof. She broke off a piece and ate it slowly, standing alone in her grandmother's kitchen, and then she photographed the empty spot where the piece had been and sent it to him with no caption at all.

activity: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
knowledge_domain: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
fact: The development typically breaks the exposition's themes into short fragments and moves them quickly through several keys, which gives the section its restless sound.
story:
The score lay open on the kitchen table beside a cold mug of tea, and Sophia had drawn three careful brackets in pencil, then erased two of them. The Mozart was the K. 333 first movement, and her assignment, due in Ms. Charles's music theory class on Friday, was to mark the exposition, the development, and the recapitulation, with measure numbers, and to defend her choices in a paragraph. She had listened to the recording four times. The opening had settled into her like weather, that bright, patient tune, but somewhere in the middle the music had turned restless, stormy, and she had lost her footing entirely.

Her phone buzzed against the table. A message from Kyla: "i've bracketed everything and it still looks wrong. did you find where the storm starts? also did ms charles say the paragraph has to defend BOTH brackets or just the weird ones?" Sophia typed back that she had no idea, that she had erased so many pencil marks the paper was going thin, and that she was going to listen again with headphones and her eyes shut, which felt less like studying and more like eavesdropping.

She pressed play and closed her eyes. The first tune returned again and again, then wandered, then broke. In the stormy middle stretch something flickered past, three or four notes that snagged in her ear like a thread caught on a nail. She sat up. She rewound. She rewound again, then a third time, chasing the fragment the way you chase a word on the tip of your tongue. It was the opening tune, or a piece of it, the first few notes, disguised, hurled through a different key, gone before she could point at it.

She found it in the score. Her pencil hovered over the measure. The opening theme, or a shard of it, buried in the turbulence. She wrote in the margin, small and crooked: it's the same tune. Broken into pieces. It moves through several keys, fast, one after another, and that's why the middle sounds restless, like it can't sit still, can't land anywhere. She stared at what she'd written. This was not in her notes from class. Ms. Charles had played the movement through once and said only, "You'll recognize more than you expect, if you listen like a detective." Sophia had thought that was a throwaway line. Now it seemed like a dare.

The phone buzzed again. Kyla: "ok update. my dad says the middle section is where the composer just does whatever he wants, no rules, that's why it sounds chaotic. he took piano for 3 years." Sophia read it twice. Part of her wanted that to be true, because it was tidy, and it would let her bracket the storm as one shapeless block and go to bed. But the fragment she'd found argued otherwise. The storm wasn't freedom from the opening material. It was the opening material, disassembled, its pieces transmuted into something anxious, hurried from key to key like a fugitive changing trains. The restlessness had a source. She wrote back: "your dad is wrong i think. the middle takes the first tune apart and scatters the pieces. i found the opening hidden inside it. like 4 notes of it. listen at 1:52 and tell me you don't hear it."

Her mother came through the kitchen, looked at the pencil-covered score, the headphones, the abandoned tea, and asked if she'd eaten. Sophia said yes, which was half true, and her mother said, "Don't stay up transmuting yourself into a zombie," misusing the word with total confidence, and Sophia laughed despite herself and said she would try to be more judicious about her evenings, though she was already reaching for the headphones again.

Here was the problem she couldn't shake. If the development was where the themes broke apart, then the recapitulation had to be where they came home, and she could hear that homecoming clearly, the return of the first tune in all its calm. But there was one passage, eight bars before the return, that she could not assign. It wasn't stormy. It wasn't the tune either. It hovered, quiet and unresolved, and she could argue it belonged to the development or to the recapitulation, and Ms. Charles would want one answer defended in one paragraph. Sophia sat with her pencil above the paper and admitted to the empty kitchen that she did not know. The music, she suspected, did not care about her brackets.

She picked up the phone and dictated a message to Kyla, because some things needed to be said in full sentences: "I'm bracketing the storm from where the tune first breaks apart to where the first theme comes back in full, and I'm writing in my paragraph that Mozart takes the exposition's themes, breaks them into short fragments, and moves them quickly through several keys, and that's what makes the development sound restless. I found the opening tune hiding inside the storm, which is how I know the middle isn't random. There's one bit before the return that I'm leaving unmarked and calling a pivot, because it's honestly both or neither, and if Ms. Charles takes marks off for that, so be it." She read it over. It sounded certain in a way she wasn't entirely, and honest in a way she was, and she could not make those two things the same thing.

Kyla replied with a voice memo. Sophia pressed play, and Kyla's voice came through fast and low: "Wait, go back, play that bit again, the one you said. Oh my god. It's there. It's the beginning. It's hiding in the storm." In the background of the recording, faint and tinny, the recording was still playing, the little fragment flickering past, and Sophia, alone in her kitchen at eleven at night, pressed her own play button and listened for it again.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: In gleaning programs, food bank volunteers harvest crops that remain in farm fields after the main harvest, food that would otherwise go to waste.
story:
The flyer had been taped to the library's front desk for two weeks before Rose actually read it, which surprised her, because she passed it every afternoon on her way to the study carrels by the window. VOLUNTEERS WANTED, it said, SATURDAY MORNING, MEET AT THE LIBRARY, DRESS FOR FIELDS. She had been telling herself all summer that she should do something that wasn't for her transcript, and then worrying that wanting it not to be for her transcript was itself a kind of calculation she couldn't escape. On the last Saturday of August she showed up at eight with her older boots in a grocery bag.

Four other people waited under the oak by the library steps. One of them was Zane, who had been in her civics class and had once argued, convincingly, that all charity was public relations. Ari was there too, wearing a sun hat and carrying two water bottles, one of which they offered to Rose immediately. The last was Mr. Hosseini, who had retired across the street from Rose's house and who she knew mainly as the man who returned her family's escaped dog with grave courtesy and no small talk.

A woman from the county food bank arrived in a white van and stood at the back of it with a clipboard. "We're gleaning today," she said. "That's the word for it. Volunteers go into farm fields after the main harvest and pick what's left." She said it plainly, the way you'd say the name of a street. Rose turned the word over while the woman went on: the farmer had already taken what he could sell, and what remained in the field was squash, thousands of pounds of it, food that would otherwise go to waste in the dirt unless they got it out that morning.

Zane raised a hand. "So the farmer couldn't be bothered to pick it himself?" The woman said the economics didn't work for a second pass through the field, and that the food bank had an agreement with him, and that they were welcome to walk if they didn't like the arrangement. Nobody walked. On the drive out, Ari asked Rose whether she'd ever been on a farm, and Rose said only in books, and Ari laughed and said that between the two of them they had plenty of erudition and no knowledge, which Rose suspected was true and didn't mind.

The field was long and brown, striped with dry vines, and the squash lay everywhere under them like dropped lanterns. Rose worked a row near Zane. The sun climbed. Her arms turned orange to the elbow, and she learned quickly to be circumspect about the wasps in the soft ones. Around ten the van's driver came down the rows calling that the truck was filling faster than expected, that they should sort harder, take only what was firm.

Zane, who by then had softened considerably and had begun to cajole a distant row of volunteers into a competition, went the other way. He started taking everything, bruised, split, half rotted, piling it in his crate with the defiant energy of someone who had just discovered a principle and refused to compromise it. Waste was waste. Leaving food in a field was a scandal. When the driver reached him and said the food bank couldn't distribute damaged produce, that it would just have to be thrown out at the other end, Zane stood in the vines with his full crate and didn't move. Rose watched from her row, breathing hard, feeling the pull of both positions and not knowing yet what she thought.

From where Zane stood, the field looked like an argument he was losing. He had spent the morning believing that he was finally doing something pure, something with no angle to it, and now a woman with a clipboard was telling him that purity rotted. He looked down the row at Rose, who had stopped picking and was looking back at him, and he thought, with some irritation, that she always looked like she was weighing things, that she would probably weigh this for a week. Then he saw her set down her crate and come over, and he braced himself for a speech.

She didn't make one. "Take the good ones from the bad ones," Rose said. "Leave the rest for the farmer. He plows it in, it goes back into the ground, it isn't wasted exactly." She had worked this out walking over, and it still felt provisional, a bridge rather than an answer, but she said it anyway. Zane crouched and began sorting, slowly at first, then faster, and by the time the truck left the field his crate held only firm squash and his hands were stained where the split ones had given way under them.

At the library that afternoon, where Mr. Hosseini had agreed to receive the overflow for the little community shelf by the photocopier, Rose stacked butternut and acorn squash into a pyramid while Ari made a sign on the back of the flyer. Mr. Hosseini examined one squash at length, turned it over, and set it back in place. Zane leaned against the desk eating an apple someone had left in the giveaway basket, and Rose caught his eye and raised the last squash in her orange hands like a toast. "Gleaned," she said.

activity: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
knowledge_domain: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
fact: Higher interest rates pay savers more, so households tend to shift some money from spending into savings, which lowers demand for goods and helps slow price rises.
story:
Henry had always considered himself good with money, which was the kind of thing a person believes right up until the moment it stops being true. The paycheck from the garden center sat in his checking account, six hundred and forty dollars he had earned by hauling mulch through the hottest July anyone in town could remember, and every evening after work he opened the banking app and looked at it the way other people looked at weather radar. He was saving, he told himself, for the phone. The screen on his current one had been cracked since spring, a webbed constellation in the upper left corner that he had learned to read around.

On Thursday he came home smelling of soil and sweat and found his mother at the kitchen table with a letter from the bank, her reading glasses low on her nose. "Did you see this?" she said, and slid it across. He said he had, though he hadn't. That was a habit of his, the small preemptive claim of already knowing, and it rarely cost him anything, so he rarely noticed it.

Koby came over that night with two energy drinks and no plans, the particular ennui of a summer stretching toward September. They sat on the garage floor because the house was too warm, and Koby talked about a girl from his shift at the pharmacy while Henry half listened and opened the app again. The savings account, the one his mother had opened for him when he was nine and he had never once transferred anything into, now paid four and a half percent. He had a vague memory of it paying almost nothing, though when he tried to recall the actual number, nothing came.

"It's the central bank," said Viviane the next afternoon, from the porch swing, when he mentioned it. She was stretched out with her feet on the railing, having appointed herself the household's only source of news since she'd started reading the business section for a class. "They raised rates. That's why savings pays more now."

"Raised rates to do what, though?" Henry asked. He genuinely wanted to know, and also wanted to seem like someone who had been following it all along.

Viviane shrugged. "Prices. Everything got expensive, so they did a thing." She wasn't going to be more help than that, and she went back to her iced coffee, and Henry sat with the word "thing" like a stone in his shoe.

He walked to the hardware store Saturday morning to buy a new nozzle for the hose, and on the way back he stopped at Ms. Augustin's because she had flagged him down from her garden, irascible as ever about the tomatoes. "Squirrel," she said, pointing at a half-eaten fruit with the outrage of a woman surveying a crime scene. He fixed her fence wire while she supervised, and he told her about the rate on his account, partly to fill the silence and partly because she was old enough to have seen many summers of prices. She said only, "My nephew moves his money whenever they do this. Says everybody's doing it." Then she paid him ten dollars for the wire, which he tried to refuse twice.

It was at home, that evening, with the phone listing open in one browser tab and the savings account in another, that the two halves finally touched. The phone cost five hundred and twenty dollars. The savings account paid four and a half percent. He did the arithmetic on paper because he didn't trust himself to do it in his head: leave the money in savings and it grew; take it out and buy the phone and it didn't. He thought about Koby, who had bought a phone in June, and about Viviane's nephew, whoever he was, moving his money like a tide. If a lot of households did this, if people shifted money from spending into savings because savings finally paid something, then fewer people were out buying things, and he understood, suddenly and incompletely, that this was the "thing," the mechanism by which raising rates was supposed to lean on prices. He could not have explained it to a classroom. He could feel it in his own hand, though, the actual choice, the rate pulling one way and the cracked screen pulling the other.

He texted Viviane: "Is that why they raise rates? People save instead of spending and then prices slow down?" She replied with a thumbs up and then, a minute later, "pretty much I think." He sat with that, honest enough with himself to know that "pretty much I think" from Viviane was not the same as knowing. Maybe it was the whole answer. Maybe it was a thread off the edge of one.

His mother called from the living room, asking if he wanted the leftovers. In a minute, he said. He looked at the transfer screen, the amount field empty, the cursor blinking, and typed in five hundred and twenty dollars, and then deleted it, and then typed it again.

activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
knowledge_domain: applying to college and waiting for the answer
fact: The FAFSA is the form US students complete to apply for federal financial aid such as Pell Grants and federal loans, and many states and colleges also use it to award their own aid.
story:
The mailbox at the end of Jacob's driveway had a dented door that stuck in damp weather, and he forced it open with his thumb every afternoon the way other people checked their phones. Inside there were usually only grocery flyers and a notice about storm drains, but today there was a fat envelope from Wexler State, the sort of envelope his counselor had told him meant good news, though Jacob had begun to distrust that folk wisdom the way he distrusted most things that sounded tidy. He stood in the driveway in his socks, because he had run out without shoes, and turned the envelope over twice without opening it.

He was sixteen, a junior who had applied to the early program mostly because Russell had dared him to, and the application had required a signature from a parent that his mother had provided with a shrug that absolved her of everything that came after. Whatever the envelope held, he would be the one holding it. He walked back up the driveway and sat on the front steps instead of going inside, and that was where Dina found him on her way home from the community college fair.

"Is that it," she said. She set her canvas bag down on the walk. Dina was a senior, and for weeks she had been talking about the same school, the same program, with the fixed attention of someone who had narrowed her whole life to one doorway. "Open it. You have to open it in front of someone, that's the rule."

"I don't accept the rule." But he said it without force. He had spent the semester arguing positions he did not quite hold, in debate club, with Russell about whether optimism was a form of dishonesty, and lately he had begun to feel that his fondness for rationalism, for reasons lined up like bricks, was a kind of armor, and that armor was not the same as a plan. Dina sat down beside him on the step.

"Can I tell you something while you decide?" she said. "We almost missed it. Me and my mom. We sat down at the computer at like eleven at night because the state deadline was coming, and we were doing the FAFSA. You know what that is?"

"The federal form," Jacob said, though he only half knew. "Something about loans."

"It's the form you fill out for federal financial aid, like Pell Grants and federal loans," Dina said. "But that's not the whole thing. The state uses it for its own aid, and colleges use it too, for theirs. So if we'd missed it, it wouldn't have just been the federal money. It would have been everything stacked on top of it. My mom kept saying we'd figure it out, and I kept saying figuring out is not a form you can submit." She laughed, but not happily. "We hit send at 11:52."

Jacob looked down at the envelope. He had not thought about money at all when he applied, which now struck him as almost deliberate, a soft brick in the wall he had built out of anything friable, anything that might crumble if he leaned on it. His mother worked at the hospital laundry. There were forms he did not know about, deadlines that existed whether or not he believed in them.

"I changed my mind, by the way," Dina said. "About Wexler. There's a program closer to home, and with the aid it might actually be less, and I can still do everything I wanted. I fought my mom about it for a month and then I just, stopped. Not gave up. Stopped fighting the math." She picked at the strap of her bag. "I still want the same life. I just found a different door into it."

Jacob worked his thumb under the flap. The letter inside was two pages, and the first line said congratulations, and then a number, a tuition figure that stood on the page like a fence. Below it, in smaller type, a sentence about aid: to be considered for federal and state assistance, complete the FAFSA. He read it twice. The congratulations and the fence were the same object, depending on which side you stood on.

"Good news?" Dina asked.

"I don't know yet," Jacob said, and it was the most honest thing he had said all week. "I got in. The rest is a form." He folded the letter along its original creases and put it back in the envelope, and then he stood and pulled the dented mailbox door open one more time to check, out of habit, for anything else. "Walk with me. I want to see what my mom says before I decide what this is."

Dina picked up her bag and followed him up the walk, and behind them the mailbox door swung slowly shut on its own weight, clicking closed against the damp.

activity: taking a first driving lesson
knowledge_domain: taking a first driving lesson
fact: A blind spot is an area around a car the driver cannot see from the seat, even with mirrors, which is why drivers turn their heads to check before changing lanes.
story:
Jessica had the keys in her fist before her father finished saying they were on the counter, and by the time he came out the front door she was already in the driver's seat, adjusting the mirror with the seriousness of a surgeon scrubbing in. Mr. Bennett's car sat in his driveway across the street, which meant he was home, which meant he would probably watch, which meant she had an audience for whatever was about to happen.

"Seatbelt," her father said, lowering himself into the passenger seat. "Mirror. Seat." He said it the way he said grace at Thanksgiving, a ritual whose meaning had worn smooth.

"Done, done, done." She had practiced this in her head all week, the whole syntax of driving, the order of operations her father had recited until it had the rhythm of a sentence she could diagram: check, signal, shoulder, go. It had seemed easy on paper, an argument with only clean premises. Now the wheel was actually under her hands and the premises felt considerably less stable.

She backed out of the driveway in a series of small, petulant lurches, the car moving like it disagreed with her, and her father's hand hovered over the dash but never landed. "Slower on the gas," he said. "It's not a race." She wanted to tell him that she knew it wasn't a race, that she had read the entire driver's manual twice, that she could recite the right-of-way rules at a roundabout, but instead she said nothing and pulled onto the street, and the car behind them kept a polite distance, and she exhaled.

They drove the long loop past the school and the shuttered hardware store and the new development where the McCalls used to have a horse pasture. Her father had her turn left at the light, then left again, then merge onto the wider road that led toward the highway frontage, and it was there, in the merge, that the world presented her with a situation her mental manual had not quite covered.

"Get into the right lane when you can," her father said, because the frontage road split ahead. Jessica checked the mirror. Empty road, silver morning, nothing coming. She flipped the turn signal on, out of pride as much as caution, and began to drift right.

"Whoa, whoa. Head. Turn your head."

A gray sedan sat beside her, close enough that she could see the driver's sunglasses, close enough that if she had moved another foot the two cars would have met along their sides like a closing book. She wrenched the wheel back into her own lane and her heart went off like a smoke alarm, and the gray sedan slid past with its driver shaking her head, and Jessica gripped the wheel and stared straight ahead at nothing.

"It was in the mirror," she said. "I looked. I looked and there was nothing there."

"That's why you turn your head," her father said, and she could hear him choosing to stay calm, which was somehow worse. "There's a blind spot. An area around the car you can't see from the seat. Even with the mirrors, it's there. That's the whole reason for the shoulder check."

She pulled into the pharmacy parking lot and set the brake and sat with both hands on the wheel. A blind spot. She turned the words over. All her life she had been told, in various forms, to trust her own perception: check your sources, verify, look with your own eyes. And here was a machine, a system, engineered by adults with degrees, that had a built-in region of invisibility, a place where looking directly at a mirror showed you a lie by omission. The mirrors had not been broken. They had simply been asked a question they could not answer, and they had answered it anyway, with blank silver confidence.

Her father was quiet for a moment, which she appreciated. Then he said, "Want to try the merge again?"

"The road splits up there."

"There's a turnaround at the gas station."

She looked at him. She was not sure she could predicate her entire driving future on one near miss, or whether that was even the right way to think about it, whether the lesson was slow down or look harder or simply accept that some things can't be seen from where you sit. Maybe all three. Maybe the honest position was that she didn't know yet, and that not knowing was itself the first thing the road required of her.

She signaled out of the lot, checked the mirror, and then, deliberately, turned her whole head and looked over her shoulder into the space the mirror couldn't tell her about. It was empty this time, sunlight and asphalt and nothing, but she looked anyway.

"Good," her father said, quietly, and she pulled back onto the road and drove toward the split.

activity: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
knowledge_domain: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
fact: Researcher Amy Edmondson described 'psychological safety' in 1999 as a team's shared belief that it is safe to take interpersonal risks, such as admitting a mistake.
story:
The party had thinned to the porch by ten, where Duncan was handing out slices of cake nobody wanted and the somnolence of a long July evening had settled over the folding chairs. Leah sat with her knees drawn up, holding a red cup of flat lemonade, and watched Chelsey across the yard telling some story with her whole body, arms carving the air. Two weeks ago Chelsey had stood in front of their debate team and read her rebuttal, and it had gone badly, and every person in that room had known it went badly, and nobody had said so. Mr. Nikolaidis, who coached them, had said only "Good effort, let's move on," and they had moved on, all the way to losing the semifinal by a margin everyone pretended not to calculate.

Leah had spent the days since then adjudicating the question in her own head, weighing silence against speech. She hadn't said anything because Chelsey was her friend, and because Chelsey was mercurial, quick to flare and quicker to go cold, and because it was easier to let the season end and let everyone carry their polite faces off to summer. But the team's collective refusal to speak had bothered her more than the loss itself. It wasn't kindness, she thought, that kept them all quiet. It was fear of looking like the one who pointed at the wound.

She had found a word for it in the college study guide her cousin left in the porch hammock. Amy Edmondson, a researcher, had described it in 1999: psychological safety, a team's shared belief that it is safe to take interpersonal risks, such as admitting a mistake. Leah read the paragraph twice while the sprinklers hissed next door, and something rearranged itself. The reason nobody had told Chelsey her rebuttal collapsed wasn't that they were nice. It was that nobody on the team believed they could risk it. And the reason Chelsey hadn't asked for help after the loss, hadn't said the obvious thing about her own performance, was probably the same.

Chelsey dropped into the chair beside her, cake balanced on a napkin. "You've been staring at me all night," she said. "Like you're deciding something."

"I am deciding something." Leah set down the cup. The yard smelled of citronella and someone's father's cigar. She could feel Duncan listening from the rail, pretending to study his phone. "About semifinals."

"Oh, we're doing this at Bianca's birthday."

"We're doing it somewhere." The words came out harder than she intended, and she softened them. "I should have said this two weeks ago, and I didn't, and that's on me. Your rebuttal was three minutes of summary. You never once answered their second argument, the one about cost, and I know you heard it because you wrote it down. I watched you write it down and then not use it."

Chelsey's jaw tightened. For a moment Leah thought she would stand, would carry the cake back into the noise and the lawn chairs. Then she said, quietly, "I froze. I looked at my notes and I couldn't find the page."

"Why didn't you say that after?"

"Because everyone was already being so nice about it." Chelsey tore the corner off her napkin. "The nice was worse. I would rather somebody just tell me."

Duncan turned around from the rail. "For the record, I froze at regionals last year and told nobody either. So it's not just you being broken, Chels." He said it lightly, but he was looking at Leah when he said it, and she understood he was doing a version of what she had just done: naming his own mistake out loud to make the ground safer for someone else.

The three of them sat while the last younger kids chased a glow stick across the dark lawn. Chelsey asked, "Next season, when one of us messes up, we just say it? Out loud, that day?"

"That day," Leah said. She was aware of how easily this could still fail, how a rule made on a porch at a birthday party might not survive a real room with real judges and a real loss, how she might be wrong that honesty and tenderness could sit in the same sentence. She didn't say any of that. Instead she picked up the untouched cake slice Duncan had left on the arm of her chair and took a bite.

"It's dry," she said, and handed it to Chelsey. "Try it anyway."

activity: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
knowledge_domain: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
fact: To compare leases fairly, add the rent to every recurring cost the tenant pays, such as heat, electricity, water, internet and insurance, to get a total monthly cost.
story:
The line at the bank moved in slow shuffles, and Maxime held the two folded lease agreements Kyler had slid across his desk that morning like evidence in a trial only Maxime seemed willing to prosecute. One was for a third-floor walk-up above a laundromat, six hundred a month, heat and water included. The other was a corner unit in a newer building five blocks east, five hundred and forty, with nothing included at all.

"You're taking the cheaper one, obviously," Kyler had said at lunch, mouth full, already spending the difference in his head. Scarlett had pulled the papers closer and frowned at them the way she frowned at badly cited essays, but she hadn't said anything, which for Scarlett was a whole argument.

Now Maxime stood behind an older man making a deposit and did what Ms. Nkosi had drilled into them all through twelfth grade: he made a list on the back of his hand. Rent. Then electricity. Then internet. Then tenant insurance, which both buildings required. The cheaper unit needed every one of them paid separately, and the more expensive one rolled heat and water into the rent. He wrote the numbers Kyler had texted him, a message still open on his phone: "electric ~ 85, internet 60 flat, insurance my cousin pays 18." Maxime added it up twice, because the first total felt like an accusation.

The tally came to seven hundred and three. The walk-up, with heat and water included, came to six hundred and seventy-eight once he added only the internet and insurance and the smaller electric bill for a building where he wouldn't be the one paying to keep the pipes warm. The cheap apartment was not the cheap apartment. Something about the arithmetic exhilarate

d him and deflated him at once: he had found the truth, and the truth cost him the corner unit with the big windows he'd already pictured Scarlett sitting in.

He remembered being nine, standing in a bank much like this one, his father crouched beside him at the counter explaining the coin rollers. "Count what's there," his father had said, sliding a roll of dimes into his palm, "not what you wish was there." Maxime had thought it was about coins for years before he understood it was never about coins.

At the writing desk by the window, where customers filled out slips of paper on a chain, he composed a message to Kyler: "Found it. To compare the leases fairly you have to add the rent to every recurring cost we'd pay, heat, electricity, water, internet, insurance, and get the total monthly cost for each place. The cheaper rent isn't the cheaper place. It's the corner unit by twenty-five a month. I'm sorry." He stared at the word sorry. It wasn't an apology, really. It was more like an acquittal he was granting himself and refusing Kyler at the same time, a verdict that let nobody off.

Kyler replied with a single eye-roll emoji and then, thirty seconds later, a longer message: "check the insurance again, my cousin's building is brick." Maxime laughed out loud, and a woman in line glanced at him. He texted back: "Brick or not, we're eighteen, our insurance is eighteen. Building doesn't change it." It was the most adult sentence he had ever typed.

Scarlett appeared at ten to four, out of breath, her bank card in her fist, deposits for the café job she'd kept all summer. She dropped into the chair beside him and read his inked hand without being asked. "So the corner unit with the rooftop thing Kyler keeps calling a terrace, it's the one that's actually cheaper," she said. Maxime nodded and turned his hand over to show the walk-up's column, its smaller total sitting there plain as a deposit slip. "The other one is cheaper," he said. "The ugly one. The one over the laundromat." Scarlett was quiet for a moment, and he could see her doing the same thing he had done, letting go of a picture she'd been keeping.

"It has a fire escape you can sit on," she said finally. "That's almost a terrace. In a hedonistic, exile kind of way." Maxime pulled the fresh application form from his folder, and before he could talk himself out of it, he wrote the laundromat address at the top, then slid the pen across the desk to her. "You put your name on it or I'm going to sit on that fire escape alone all year."

activity: how a poll's margin of error and sample size limit what its numbers can say
knowledge_domain: how a poll's margin of error and sample size limit what its numbers can say
fact: When a candidate's lead is smaller than the margin of error, the poll cannot say with confidence who is ahead, but that does not mean the race is exactly tied.
story:
The line outside the fire hall stretched past the bike racks when Ella joined it at six forty, twenty minutes before the polls closed. She had spent the whole day at the campaign office on Miller Street, and the last task of the shift had been the argument she still could not get out of her head.
