Gwen and Ilias had stood over the clipboard with the day's tracking numbers, both of them raising their voices over the phone bank chatter, and neither of them had noticed Ella come back in from the coffee run.

"It's a tie," Gwen had said, tapping the page. "Forty-nine to forty-seven. That's within the margin of error, so it's a tie."

"That's not what within the margin of error means," Ilias had said. "It means the poll can't say who's ahead. That's different from saying nobody's ahead."

Gwen had rolled her eyes at him and started reciting the script for the last call push, and that was supposed to be the end of it, except that the office manager had asked for volunteers to hand out sample ballots at the fire hall until closing. Gwen had claimed the drive over to the polling station gave them time to settle it, and Ella, holding the thermos she never got to deliver, had been appointed judge. The verdict was due, by Gwen's own ruling, before the doors shut at eight.

The line moved in surges. Ahead of Ella, an old man leaned on a cane and a younger woman held his elbow; behind her, two poll workers on their break talked about which precinct ran out of the big-print ballots first. Gwen and Ilias were already at the front of the fire hall, planted on either side of a folding table stacked with literature, and they were still at it.

"Three points is the margin," Gwen said when Ella reached them. "The lead is two. Two is smaller than three. Tie."

"Say the true lead is two and the poll is perfect," Ilias said. "The poll still says two. It still can't tell them apart. It's not measuring nothing."

Ella handed out a sample ballot to a woman in a rain jacket and thought about the thermos, which she had left on the office counter. She had spent four Saturdays canvassing, and on every door she had said some version of "it's close," and she had never once asked herself what she meant by close. She had meant the feeling of it, the tightness in the office when the numbers came in. That was not the same as knowing.

"If it can't say who's ahead," Gwen said, "then for all you know it's a tie."

"No. It means the poll can't say with confidence who's ahead," Ilias said. "Not that they're exactly even. One of them could really be up by two, or up by four, or down by one. The poll just can't pin it down."

Gwen turned to Ella with her palm flat on the table, and behind her the clock over the fire chief's door read seven thirty-five. "Settle it. He's being bombastic. It's a two-point race in a poll with a three-point margin. Call it a tie so we can stop arguing and go vote."

Ella looked down the line, which the poll workers were now walking to count heads, making sure everyone queued before eight would get in. She thought about the doors she had knocked on, how she had reported each one to the clipboard as a number, one more data point in a stack, and how the stack had never once said anything clean. A poll that said forty-nine and forty-seven with a margin of three was like a person squinting at two objects almost side by side and reporting that they looked like one. It was honest about its own eyesight. It was not a photograph.

"He's right," Ella said. "Not that it's a tie. The lead is smaller than the margin, so the poll can't say who's ahead. But that doesn't mean the race is exactly tied. Somebody might really be ahead. The poll just can't tell us which one."

Gwen stared at her. "So the poll says nothing."

"It says it's close," Ella said. "That's all we've actually known this whole month. We kept acting like we knew more."

The clock touched seven fifty. The three of them took their places at the back of the line behind the man with the cane, and Gwen was quiet for almost a full minute, which was, Ella thought, possibly a first. Then Gwen said, "So tomorrow, when the numbers come in, we still won't know," and Ilias said, "We'll know tonight," and pointed at the fire hall doors, and the line shuffled forward into the gymnasium, where the voting booths stood in two rows under the basketball net, and the poll worker with the binder found Ella's name and read it aloud.

activity: to explain comparative advantage and why two countries both gain from trading
knowledge_domain: to explain comparative advantage and why two countries both gain from trading
fact: Trade based on comparative advantage raises a country's total income, but individual workers in industries that now face cheaper imports can still lose their jobs or wages.
story:
Jacob had promised Ms. Nur a five-minute explanation of comparative advantage by tomorrow morning, and so far his notebook held a diagram of two countries, two arrows, and a growing suspicion that he didn't understand it at all. He sat at the kitchen table with the window open, listening to his grandfather move around the living room, arranging and rearranging the same three magazines. The apartment smelled of burnt coffee and the lemon polish his grandfather insisted on even now.

"Your mother says you have a speech," his grandfather said from the doorway, and Jacob nodded without looking up. "About trade. Trade with other countries." He said it the way he might have said "about the weather on Mars."

"It's for economics. Ms. Nur wants us to explain why two countries both gain from trading, even when one of them is better at making everything." Jacob rotated the notebook so the arrows faced outward. "It's called comparative advantage. Each country makes the thing it's least bad at, relatively speaking, and they swap, and both end up with more."

His grandfather pulled out the opposite chair and sat down heavily, as though the sentence had weight. He was a quiet man these days, but Jacob had a presentiment, watching him fold his hands, that the quiet was about to end. "You want to know who ends up with more," his grandfather said. "Come downstairs with me."

They took the elevator to the basement, where his grandfather kept a locked cabinet he almost never opened. Inside was a small steel toolbox, a union pin, and a folded photograph of a factory floor with maybe forty men squinting into the sun. He laid the photograph on top of the dryer and put one thick finger on a young man in the second row, a man with Jacob's same heavy eyebrows. "Twenty-six years I worked in that building. Then one year the orders went somewhere cheaper, and the building went dark. I drove past it last month. There's a gym in half of it now." He tapped the photograph again. "So when you say both countries gain, tell me which part of this country gained what."

Jacob looked at the young man in the second row for a long moment. He thought of Jaiveer, whose father imported machine parts and had recently expanded his warehouse, and of Angel, who worked weekends at a store whose entire inventory arrived in containers from overseas, cheap enough that she and her cousins could actually buy things. Both of those things were true. He could feel both of them in his hands at once, like two objects of different temperatures.

"The whole country's income goes up," Jacob said slowly, testing each word as he set it down. "That part is real. Total income rises. But that doesn't mean every person in it is better off. The workers in the industries that suddenly face cheaper imports, they can lose their jobs. Or their wages." He heard himself say it and realized it was the first sentence all evening he actually believed. "I was going to stand up there and say everybody wins. That's not what it says. It says the country wins on net, and some people inside it pay for that."

His grandfather was quiet, but his shoulders had come down an inch, and he smoothed the photograph with the side of his thumb. "So who pays," he said, not really asking. "Somebody always pays." He folded the picture along its old creases, creases so worn they had become a kind of hinge, and Jacob thought about how a person could spend decades resuscitating a self a decision made in another country had quietly ended. He didn't say that out loud. He said, "Can I borrow the photograph? Just for tonight. I'll bring it back before you're up."

Upstairs, he texted Jaiveer, who replied with three paragraphs defending his father's warehouse, then texted Angel, who replied that her store would close without imports and so would her Saturdays. Jacob read both messages, then turned his phone face down and rewrote the first line of his notes. Somewhere in the middle of drafting, his grandfather's bellicose old radio, left on the counter, crackled through the wall with a talk-show host shouting about trade wars, and Jacob got up and turned it off, because the shouting wasn't the point either. Ms. Nur wanted five minutes; he had until morning; and he now had a diagram, a photograph, and a sentence he couldn't make neat no matter how he arranged it.

He practiced once in the mirror, holding the photograph beside his face, saying, "The country gains, and the man in the second row loses his job, and both of those are true at once." It sounded unfinished. It was unfinished. He set the photograph on the table, propped against the sugar bowl, so it would be the first thing he saw in the morning, and turned off the kitchen light.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: After a concussion, athletes return through graduated steps from rest to full play, moving to the next step only while they stay free of symptoms.
story:
The community center gym smelled of floor wax and old rubber, and Sarah had come to think of it as the only place where the weeks of her last season at home had a shape. She was a senior, a midfielder on the indoor soccer league Ms. Mori had run for eleven years, and she wanted one full season without anything going wrong. Elodie wanted the same thing, though for Elodie the wanting had a sharper edge, because Elodie had spent the first three weeks of the season not playing at all.

After Elodie's concussion, the doctor had given her a plan that Ms. Mori taped inside her clipboard: return through graduated steps, starting with rest and ending with full play, and moving to the next step only while she stayed free of symptoms. Elodie had recited it in the car like a catechism her mother was trying to inculcate, laughing a little as she said it, and Sarah had laughed too, because Elodie laughed at everything, including things that frightened her. Rest, then light activity, then sport-specific drills without contact, then full contact, then full play. One step at a time, and only if the headache stayed away.

That night the gym was hot and the lights buzzed. Elodie had been cleared for sport-specific drills, no contact, and she moved through the passing patterns with her old smoothness, calling for the ball in her low voice. Jensen, who had driven them all season and who kept a folded schedule of Elodie's steps in his visor, kept glancing over whenever she jogged. Sarah kept glancing too, less casually, because that was the arrangement they had never spoken aloud: watch her, and don't make watching a thing.

Halfway through the session, Elodie took a ball off her thigh and turned upfield, and Sarah saw her stop mid-stride, one hand drifting to her temple, fingers pressing the skin above her eyebrow. She kept playing for another minute. Then she walked to the sideline and sat down on the folded mats, elbows on her knees.

"You okay?" Jensen asked, already crouching beside her, and Sarah heard the question he was actually asking, which was whether they should pretend.

"Headache," Elodie said. "It's back."

Sarah sat down on her other side. She knew what the plan said, because Elodie had made her read it twice: you moved to the next step only while you stayed free of symptoms. The words had sounded simple in the car. Here, with two league games left and the playoffs after that, they were not simple at all. "Light drills," Sarah said slowly, working it out as she spoke. "So you step back a stage. You go back a step and hold there until it clears."

"I know," Elodie said. She was looking at the floor, her thumb tracing the seam of her sock.

The coach wanted to sub her back in for the scrimmage, waving from across the gym, saying she looked fine to him, and Sarah felt the pull of that, the idea that sitting out one drill was caution carried to the point of speciousness, rules invented to protect people from nothing. She almost believed it for a second, because wanting Elodie on the field was its own argument. But the plan wasn't an argument, and it wasn't caution dressed up as wisdom. It was a sequence, and the sequence only worked going forward when nothing pulled it backward. She stood up and walked over to the coach and said, quietly, that Elodie's headache had come back during the light drills and she had to drop back a stage, and the coach's mouth opened and closed, and he nodded.

Ms. Mori brought Elodie water and sat with her while the scrimmage ran, asking about her college applications, which was a way of asking about her head without asking about her head. Sarah noticed that, and noticed too how Jensen kept the folded schedule out of his visor for the rest of the night, checking it like a bus timetable, as if the steps might rearrange themselves when no one was looking. She thought, watching them, that she had learned two things at once that season: that rules could be cages built by people who had never been inside one, and that some rules were the opposite, ladders you climbed only as fast as your body allowed, and that telling one from the other was work nobody could do for you. She could not yet say, honestly, which category her own certainty fell into. She only knew that Elodie was upright and joking by the water fountain, and that the season had two games left, and that whether Elodie would reach the last step in time was a question no one in the gym could answer.

After practice, Sarah gathered the cones while Jensen held the door and Elodie waited in the cold with her hood up. "Next week I start the stage over," Elodie said. "Light drills again."

"I know," Sarah said. She stacked the last cone, shouldered the bag, and followed them out.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: US food safety guidance says perishable food should not sit between 40 and 140 degrees Fahrenheit for more than two hours, or one hour when it is above 90 degrees.
story:
Gabrielle arrived at the farmers' market with her grandmother's canvas bag and a plan that she had written on her wrist in gel pen, which was already smearing. Chicken, her mother had said. Something with chicken, because it was her turn to cook and her brother would complain about anything that required chewing. She found the poultry stand first, then spent forty minutes arguing with herself over apricots, and by the time she got home, the bag had ridden around in the hot trunk of the car for the length of a long phone call from Annie about whether Annie's crush had waved at her or at the person behind her.

"Two and a half hours," her mother said at the counter, not accusing, just noting, the way she noted things. "And it's ninety-one degrees out."

"It was in the trunk."

"I know it was in the trunk."

Gabrielle stood there holding the chicken, which had gone slack in its paper wrapping, and felt the particular shame of someone who has just been told a fact she half-knew. She set it down and pulled out her phone. Annie answered on the second ring, because Annie always answered as though the phone were on fire.

"Is my chicken dead," Gabrielle said. "Like, dead-dead. ruined-dead."

"What did you do to the chicken?"

"Nothing. It sat in the trunk. My mom says the rule is perishables can't sit between forty and a hundred forty degrees for more than two hours, or just one hour if it's over ninety out."

"Where did your mom get that?"

"It's food safety guidance. It's official. It's on the internet wearing a little badge." She looked out the window at the heat shimmering off the driveway. "And it is, I want to say, resolutely above ninety today."

Annie made a sympathetic noise. "So one hour. How long was the trunk situation?"

"Two and a half. Maybe two and forty."

"Gabs."

"I was deciding about apricots. There was a moment where I was deciding about apricots."

She threw the chicken away, which felt like eviscerating her own afternoon, and then stood in front of the open fridge with the apricots, which had also been in the trunk, and thought: these are not chicken. Stone fruit is sturdier. But how much sturdier? The guidance said perishable food, and an apricot seemed less perishable than chicken, but she had no rule for apricots, only vibes, and vibes had already killed one bird today.

Her brother drifted in and ate a plum from the bag while she deliberated. "These are fine," he said, with his mouth full, which she noted was not evidence of anything except his confidence.

Mr. Bautista, the neighbor, was watering his tomatoes when she went out to ask him, because he was the kind of man who knew things and enjoyed being asked, though she was careful to frame it as a hypothetical so he could not mount a lecture. "Hypothetically," she said, "if apricots sat in a hot car for two and a half hours."

"Hypothetically," he said, "I'd eat them tonight or not at all, and I'd cut out anything soft." He turned off the hose. "You cooking?"

"Chicken," she said, and then, at his face, "new chicken. Store chicken. Emergency chicken."

That evening she roasted the emergency chicken with the apricots, halved, their soft parts carved away, and her brother ate two servings and her mother went back for skin, and Gabrielle sat at the table feeling both clever and not entirely sure the cleverness was earned. The rule was clear about two hours and clear about one hour above ninety, but the apricots had occupied a gap in the rule, a place where the guidance went quiet and a person had to decide alone, and she had decided, and everyone was alive, which proved little either way. When Annie texted later, "did everyone survive dinner or are you a local news story," Gabrielle typed back "survived, no thanks to me," then deleted "no thanks to me" and wrote "apricots ruled" instead, because ruling was nearer the truth, and confidence, she was learning, was mostly a thing you did on purpose.

Later, drying the last pan, she found herself changing her mind about something smaller: that her mother's noting-things-at-the-counter tone was not surveillance but mercy, a way of saying a fact without saying a punishment. She texted her mother, who was upstairs, "thank you for not making the chicken a whole thing," and got back a single thumbs-up.

"Next time I buy ice," she said out loud, to the pan, to the apricot pits in the compost, to nobody.

"Gabs," her brother called from the living room, "there's a peach left."

activity: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
knowledge_domain: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
fact: High blood pressure often causes no symptoms at all, which is why it is called a silent killer and is found mainly by measuring it.
story:
The cuff hissed and tightened around her grandmother's arm until the old woman winced, then released its grip in slow, reluctant increments, as though it disliked giving up its answer. Annabelle copied the numbers onto the kitchen notepad, 158 over 96, and beneath them wrote the words she'd memorized from the worksheet Ms. Morales had handed out on Friday: normal, elevated, stage one, stage two. The worksheet had a decision tree on the back, branches for diet and exercise and sodium, and Annabelle had promised to present it to the health class on Tuesday, which was why the cuff, borrowed from the school nurse, was on the kitchen table beside the sugar bowl.

"That machine is being dramatic," her grandmother said. She reached for her coffee. "I feel fine, so it's fine. Your grandfather's cuff never said anything like that."

Annabelle laid her hand flat over the numbers so her grandmother couldn't read them upside down, a gesture she recognized, too late, as its own small dishonesty. "Do you actually feel different when it's high?" she asked. "Like, is there a feeling?"

"There'd have to be a feeling. Everything wrong with me announces itself. My knee announces itself every morning."

Annabelle turned the notepad around. She had read the phrase four times in the packet and underlined it twice, and now she said it the way you'd say a rumor you'd checked yourself. "It's called a silent killer. High blood pressure. It doesn't cause symptoms, most of the time, so people don't know unless they measure it."

Her grandmother set the coffee down without drinking. "Whose words are those?"

"Mine. From the packet." Annabelle waited, because Ms. Morales had a rule about waiting after you said a hard thing, and because she didn't trust herself not to fill the silence with something soft and useless.

Her grandmother looked at the numbers on the pad for a long moment. "Your mother worries enough for three women," she said finally. "We'll measure it again tomorrow before anyone externalizes anything over the phone."

That night Annabelle sat on her bed with the packet and her phone propped against a pillow, texting Fatima, who wanted the nurse's aide certification more than she wanted prom, more, probably, than she wanted her driver's license. Fatima had been the one who claimed the blood pressure station during their practice hour and refused to give it up until her readings matched the nurse's twice in a row.

The message thread read like a small debate conducted in bursts. Fatima wrote that one reading means nothing, everyone knows that, white coat effect, caffeine, a bad night's sleep; Annabelle wrote back that two days of readings meant something, and that her grandmother had skipped her walks since winter because of the ice and then just never started again. Fatima replied with the string of steps she'd been taught: same time each day, feet flat, arm supported at heart level, no talking, and then, in a separate bubble, a sentence Annabelle read three times: "The hard part isn't the technique. The hard part is that the person has to decide their feeling fine isn't evidence." She typed "she's not bellicose, she's just stubborn," and before she could explain the word, Fatima had already sent back a thumbs up and "same thing in my house."

Conrad came over Sunday, ostensibly to study for the same presentation, actually to eat the lemon cake Annabelle's mother had left on the counter. He wanted the mark, openly and without embarrassment; he'd told the whole class he needed an A in health to offset chemistry, and he'd said it the way other people said they needed an umbrella. He read the worksheet aloud while Annabelle took her grandmother's pressure again, and when the cuff finished, he read the numbers off the little screen before anyone could stop him. 154 over 94.

"Is that bad?" her grandmother asked him, not Annabelle.

"It's a category," Annabelle said, before Conrad could improvise. "Stage two. Which is a word, not a verdict." She was aware of choosing calm, and aware that calm was partly performance, and unsure whether that made it a lie.

Conrad, chewing cake, pointed at the decision tree. "So this part, where it says diet, the sodium thing. Your grandmother cooks everything from scratch. That's supposed to be the good kind."

"She cooks from scratch with a heavy hand," her grandmother said from the chair. "Salt is the only thing I've never had to be careful with."

Annabelle wrote that down too, because it was exactly the kind of detail the packet's neat branches didn't have. The worksheet could say reduce sodium and increase activity and it would all be true, but the branches didn't know that her grandmother's walks had stopped because of ice, and that her salt was a kind of freedom she'd earned at eighty-one and wasn't planning to surrender to a worksheet. Sitting between the two, the paper's clean logic and the woman in the chair, Annabelle understood that her presentation couldn't just repeat the branches. It had to admit where they bent.

"Ms. Morales says genes load the gun," Conrad offered. "Something about genotype. Environment pulls the trigger. She says it about everything."

"That's a real thing," Annabelle said slowly. "But we don't know her genotype. We know her readings." She looked at her grandmother. "What we know is two days of numbers and how you feel, and the numbers are the part that doesn't lie about itself. That's the whole point of measuring. I can't tell you it means anything about tomorrow. I can tell you it means something about the salt."

Her grandmother laughed, then stopped laughing, then looked at the notepad again. "You'll take it again tomorrow," she said. It was not quite a question. "And you'll show me where it says how much walking."

Annabelle found the page, folded the corner, and slid the cuff back into its case. Her grandmother picked up the lemon cake knife and cut two more slices, one for each of them, and set the smaller one in front of Annabelle. "We'll start the walking Monday," she said. "You'll need the practice for your little speech."

activity: professional tone, structured writing and respectful disagreement in formal communication
knowledge_domain: professional tone, structured writing and respectful disagreement in formal communication
fact: 'Bottom Line Up Front', or BLUF, is a US military writing standard that puts the main point or request in the first lines of a message, before the supporting details.
story:
The volunteer office at the community center smelled of toner and old coffee, and Jackson had been assigned the email account because he was the only one who hadn't complained about it. Across the desk, Summer was stuffing envelopes with a speed that seemed personal, and Presley was reading the volunteer schedule upside down, looking for his own name. The coordinator, a dour man named Mr. Robinson, appeared at eleven with a stack of paper and a question.

"Has anyone answered the county office about the food drive?" he asked. "They need our request by three o'clock today, or we lose the truck."

Jackson pulled up the draft. He had written four paragraphs the night before, starting with the history of the drive, then the weather, then a worry about parking, and somewhere in the last paragraph, the actual request for the truck and driver. He read it again and felt his face warm. It was like a house where the door was hidden behind shrubs. He wondered how many emails got lost that way, buried alive in their own context.

"I don't think this is any good," he said.

Summer leaned over. "It's polite. That's something."

"Politeness isn't the problem. The problem is you have to dig for the point." He turned to Presley. "What do you notice first?"

Presley squinted. "That you like the word 'furthermore.'"

Jackson laughed despite the deadline pressing on all of them. He thought of his brother, who was in the Army and complained about emails that made him hunt for the request. He began typing a new first line: We are requesting one truck and one driver for the food drive on Saturday, June 8, from 8 a.m. to 2 p.m. Everything else, the history, the parking, the grateful paragraph, would follow underneath, demoted to supporting detail. It felt almost rude, like answering a question before it was asked.

"My brother calls that BLUF," Presley said, watching the screen. "Bottom Line Up Front. It's a US military writing standard, puts the main point in the first lines, before the details."

"So the Army figured out what I just figured out badly," Jackson said.

Summer had stopped stuffing envelopes. "But Mr. Robinson likes the formal tone. The whole 'Dear Esteemed Partners' thing. If you chop it down to the request, won't it read as cold?" She wasn't arguing to be difficult; Jackson could hear the real question in it, the competing values laid out like two roads.

He sat with that for a moment, cursor blinking. Then he kept the salutation, kept the thank-you, kept the respectful closing. He only moved the request to the front and let the rest stand behind it like evidence. Tone and structure, he thought, were not actually enemies; you could be warm and be clear, the way a good teacher could be kind and still tell you the assignment was due Friday. He read the final version aloud, quietly, testing each sentence for its weight.

At 2:40 he sent it. Mr. Robinson came back at 2:55, read the printed copy, and said nothing for a long moment, which from him might have been praise. "The county clerk replied already," he finally said. "Truck confirmed. Eight o'clock Saturday." He set the paper down with a care that seemed to burnish it somehow, an ordinary printout turned into a small success.

Later, locking up, Summer asked whether it would always work, leading with the point. Jackson shrugged and said he didn't know; some messages probably needed the winding road, some reader who wanted to be walked slowly toward the thing being asked. He only knew that today, with a deadline at three, the front door had been better than the shrubs. Presley jangled the keys and held the door.

"Saturday, eight a.m.," Presley said. "Bring gloves."

activity: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
knowledge_domain: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
fact: Upstage means away from the audience and downstage means toward it; the terms come from old raked stages that sloped down toward the audience.
story:
The gym smelled of floor wax and old paint by the time Alexander unrolled the masking tape across the boards. Ms. Kobayashi had given him the auditorium stage after school on Tuesdays and Thursdays, one-act play, his choice of script, his responsibility. He had chosen a thirty-minute piece about two brothers dividing their dead father's tools, mostly because it had only three characters and he believed, perhaps wrongly, that fewer actors meant fewer arguments.

On the first Tuesday, Ivan stood at the back wall of the stage and refused to move when Alexander asked him to come forward. "Why do you keep saying downstage?" Ivan said, not moving. "We're on a flat floor. There's no down here. There's no up."

"Upstage means away from the audience and downstage means toward it," Alexander said, and then stopped, because Ivan was already opening his mouth to ask the obvious question, and Alexander realized he did not know the answer either. He stood there in the middle of the taped rectangle with his binder against his chest. "The terms come from old raked stages," he said slowly, testing it as he went. "Stages that sloped down toward the audience. So the back really was up." He had read it somewhere, maybe in the stagecraft book Ms. Kobayashi lent him, maybe in a footnote he'd half absorbed, and only now, saying it out loud on a flat modern floor, did the geometry click into place. Ivan walked downstage, toward the empty seats, and something in Alexander's chest loosened.

Mattea played the younger brother, and she was better than either of them had expected. She found the moment in the second scene where she could turn her back on Ivan and let the audience watch her face instead, and Alexander, watching from the fourth row, saw that blocking was not traffic control. It was choosing whose face the audience got to study. He began to think of the stage as a slope anyway, invisible now but still shaping everything: whoever stood upstage of someone else was literally above them, and the audience felt that as power even if they didn't know why.

The problems arrived on schedule. The coach wanted the gym for badminton on Thursdays, so Ms. Kobayashi negotiated them into the cafeteria, where the lighting was fluorescent and merciless, and where the tape left marks on the tile that the janitor complained about in writing. The drama club's small disbursement for the production, forty dollars from the student council, went to two work lamps and a carton of apples for the prop basket, and Alexander kept the receipt in the binder because nobody else would. Ivan twisted his ankle at a pickup game and needed two weeks to recuperate, and for those two weeks Alexander ran the scenes with a borrowed actor, a quiet girl from his chemistry class who read Ivan's lines flat and stood where told, and the difference taught Alexander more than any book. The play wasn't in the words. It was in the specific bodies the words happened to.

He also learned that directing cost him something. Ivan and Mattea started deferring to him outside rehearsal, in the hallway, at lunch, as though he had become a person who knew where people should stand. He didn't. He knew where these two people should stand in this one room for thirty minutes, and even that was provisional, revised nightly in pencil. When Mattea argued that her final monologue should be delivered downstage center, alone under the work lamp, he wanted to say yes because she was probably right, and also because he was tired of deciding. He made himself argue back. He moved her upstage instead, into the shadow at the back wall, so that the audience would have to lean forward and work for her voice, and when she tried it she went silent for a moment and then said, "Oh," which was better than any compliment.

The disagreement they never settled was the ending. In the script, the brothers either reconcile or they don't, depending on how a shared glance is timed, and the playwright had refused to specify. Mattea thought the glance should come after the lights faded, so it was a rumor rather than a fact. Ivan thought it should come before, so the audience got to keep it. Alexander listened to both of them on the cafeteria floor under the humming lights, the apples going soft in their prop basket, and understood that he had to choose, and that choosing meant closing a door the playwright had deliberately left open. He had become the kind of person who closes doors, at least for half an hour at a time, and he wasn't sure yet whether that was authority or damage.

Performance night, the auditorium again, borrowed from the drama club's mainstage production during its dark week. Sixty people, more than he'd imagined, fewer than he'd hoped. The taped lines held. Ivan, still favoring the ankle, turned his limp into the older brother's limp, a limp that belonged to the father, and Alexander watched from the back of the house and felt the hair rise on his arms. During the final monologue Mattea stood in her shadow and the audience did lean forward, the whole room tilting toward her like an alluvial plain slopes to the sea, and her voice was small and sufficient.

The lights faded on the ending Alexander had chosen, Ivan's ending, the glance before the dark. In the wings afterward, hugging, sweaty, already arguing about where to get food, Ivan glanced once at Mattea across the emptying stage, a quick look Alexander almost missed, a different glance than the one in the play, and Alexander stood in the doorway with his binder under his arm and could not tell what it meant, or whether it was for Mattea, or whether it was for him, or whether some things are only ever staged in one direction, downstage toward whoever is watching.

activity: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
knowledge_domain: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
fact: A straw man is the fallacy of attacking a weaker, distorted version of someone's argument instead of the argument they actually made, while acting as if the two are the same.
story:
John had wanted the seat by the window, but Marisa took it before the bell, so he sat across from her and Helena with his binder open to a page he had titled, in pencil, "Things I Actually Believe." Mr. Hoffmann had proposed the question on Monday: if a technology existed that could safely edit human genes before birth, should parents be allowed to use it? Marisa, who wanted to be a geneticist, had spent two evenings reading about it, and today she opened with a position she had written out carefully. She was not against the technology. She was against leaving the decision entirely to individual parents, because, she said, parents acting separately would tend to choose the same few things, height and appearance mostly, and that narrowing would show up in the whole population over time, a shared phenotype that nobody had voted for.

Helena leaned forward almost before Marisa finished. "So you think the government should raise everyone's children," she said. "You think parents who want the best for their kids are basically shopping for designer babies, and everybody else just has to accept whatever some committee decides is good enough." She went on in that vein for a full minute, about bureaucrats, about conformity, about a world where everyone was engineered to be the same. She was fast and articulate, and John watched Marisa's face tighten, watched her flip her paper over as though it had become useless.

"I didn't say any of that," Marisa said. "I said parents choosing separately could still produce a shared result. That's different from saying the government should choose."

"You obviously think somebody has to control it," Helena said, "or none of it makes sense."

Mr. Hoffmann, who had been writing on the board, turned around. "Before we go on, I want each of you to state the other person's position back to them, in a form they would accept." He said it mildly and resumed writing, as if it were a small logistical matter.

Marisa went first, repeating Helena's view with surprising care: that individual liberty mattered here, that any gatekeeper could be captured or incompetent, that the risk of a bad authority exceeded the risk of scattered choices. Helena nodded. Then it was her turn. She started to say "Marisa thinks we should all be the same," and stopped, because even as she said it she could hear that Marisa had never said it. "Okay," Helena said slowly, "you think uncoordinated choices add up to a coordinated effect. Which is actually a harder argument to answer." Her ears had gone pink. John, who had been rooting quietly for Helena all week, felt something shift in him, an obligation he had not expected: she had won the exchange, in the ordinary social sense, and lost the argument, and pretending otherwise would have been gratuitous cruelty toward Marisa, who had done the reading.

At home that evening, John lay on his bed with the class handout Mr. Hoffmann had left on the corner of his desk, a photocopy of a page listing common fallacies. Near the bottom was the phrase he wanted. He read it three times, then set the page on his chest and stared at the ceiling, running the afternoon back like film. There were two arguments in the room, one Marisa's and one Helena's, and Helena had beaten the second one and behaved throughout as though it were the first. He thought about how easy it would have been to do the same thing himself. He had almost said, during the exchange, "so you trust the government more than parents," which was the same move in cheaper clothing. What he could not yet decide was whether Helena had done it on purpose. He believed she hadn't. He believed she had heard the first sentence, built the rest herself, and then answered her own construction with genuine force. That was somehow worse, because it meant the mistake was available to anyone, including him, including right now, in the dark.

The next afternoon it was Helena who found John at his locker, before philosophy, shoulder against the metal door. "That was a straw man," she said. "Yesterday. Mine." John said he'd thought so too, and told her about the handout, and she asked to see it, so they walked to the room early and read the page together by the window where Marisa usually sat.

She had arrived before either of them. Marisa looked up from her notes, and John felt the moment arrange itself: here was his want, the one he had only now recognized, to bring the two of them back into the same argument rather than two separate ones. "Helena has something," he said, and then made himself stop talking.

"I attacked a version of your view that you never held," Helena said. "The designer-baby committee thing. And I acted like it was yours. That wasn't fair, and it also wasn't smart, because your actual point, the thing about separate choices making a shared result, is the part I still can't answer." She turned the handout toward Marisa. "John found the name for it."

Marisa read the page, then looked at Helena for a long second, deciding something. "Then answer the real one," she said, and pulled her chair around so the three seats faced each other, and tapped the empty desk beside her.

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: In Arthur Aron's 1997 study, pairs of strangers took turns asking each other 36 questions that grew gradually more personal, and they ended up feeling closer than pairs making small talk.
story:
The bleachers smelled like spilled hot chocolate and cold metal, and Hunter kept his hands in his pockets because he didn't know what else to do with them. The girl beside him, whose name was certainly Maya though he was afraid to say it too often in case he was wrong about the spelling, had come with him to the homecoming game because he'd asked her under the stairwell on Tuesday and she'd said yes before he'd finished the sentence. That had been the easy part. Now the second quarter was dragging, the score was 21 to 3, and they had run out of things to say about the weather and the halftime band.

Before he'd left the house, his mother had handed him a folded piece of paper. "Maya's mother gave me this for you at pickup," she said, which was its own small mystery, since neither of them had explained how the mothers had coordinated. In the truck he'd unfolded it. The note read: "I hear you're taking my daughter to the game. She likes the ferris wheel at the fall fair and she pretends she doesn't. If the game is boring, that's on you. Signed, a woman who remembers being seventeen." He had read it three times, laughing a little, then folded it into his wallet like it was currency from a country he was about to visit.

Down on the track, Gurshaan was hauling a tripod along the sideline. He'd told Hunter at lunch that he was filming the halftime show for his application to a film program upstate, some portfolio thing, and that he needed Ms. Paquette to write about it afterward because she'd once published an essay on documentary framing in an actual journal. Gurshaan's want was simple and enormous: he wanted out of this town with evidence in his hands. He waved up at the bleachers without stopping, already counting the minutes of light left in the sky.

"It's loud," Maya said, apropos of nothing, and Hunter agreed that it was, and then they watched the punt.

He couldn't stand another quarter of this. "Can I tell you something weird I read?" he said finally, and she turned toward him with what looked like relief. "In 1997 this psychologist, Arthur Aron, did a study. Pairs of strangers took turns asking each other thirty-six questions, and the questions got gradually more personal. And afterward those pairs ended up feeling closer than pairs who just made small talk."

"Thirty-six," she said, like she was weighing it. "Do you know them?"

"Some. I found the list. I mean, I didn't print it out or anything. That would be creepy. I read it once." He felt his ears go hot in the cold. "We could try a couple. If the game stays this bad."

She pulled her scarf up to her chin, which hid whatever her mouth was doing. "Question one, then."

"What would constitute a perfect day for you?" he asked, and she actually thought about it, chin tilted, eyes on the far goalposts, and when she answered she started with waking up late and ended somewhere near the ferris wheel at the fall fair, which she claimed she'd only ridden once and not liked, and he said nothing, and kept her mother's secret like a stone in his pocket.

The band spilled onto the field at halftime, brass flashing under the lights, and Gurshaan crouched with his camera while Jaiveer held a clipboard and called out formations. Hunter and Maya kept trading questions through the noise, leaning closer to be heard. She asked him when he'd last sung to himself, and he told the truth, in the truck, that afternoon, badly. He asked her what friendship meant to her, and she said she was still deciding, that her mother had taken a sabbatical from work that spring and come back different, and Maya wasn't sure yet whether that was something to want for herself or be afraid of. He hadn't known you could be honest about not knowing. He'd been treating the whole evening like a machine with a correct setting, and here she was letting the wiring show.

Somewhere down the row, Ms. Paquette was buying popcorn from the booster stand, and Gurshaan abandoned his tripod to intercept her, holding out his phone with the footage already cued, saying something Hunter couldn't hear over the drums. Everyone, it turned out, was negotiating under these lights.

By the fourth quarter they were on a question about what he would save from a burning house, and he said the wallet, and she raised an eyebrow, and he didn't explain. He was still holding the spartan version of himself he'd practiced in the mirror, the one with plans, against this other way of doing things, one question at a time, no script, and he could not yet say which one was truer or whether they might transmute into each other if he let them. Maybe the study was right and maybe it was only a study. The scoreboard buzzer went off, the crowd surged to its feet around them, and Maya pulled her glove off and set her bare hand on the cold bench between them.

activity: graduating from high school
knowledge_domain: graduating from high school
fact: The US average adjusted cohort graduation rate for public high school students was 87 percent in the 2021-22 school year.
story:
Landon's mother had taped the banner to the living room wall with the same optimism she brought to everything, CONGRATS GRADU2024 in gold letters that were already curling at the corners. The house smelled like hot dogs and someone's cologne, and the screen door opened and shut with the rhythm of a party that had not yet decided whether it was a success. Landon stood near the guacamole with his cap in his hand and watched Jett attempt to explain flip cup to Emilie's younger cousin, who was twelve and unimpressed.

He had invited forty-one people on the group chat. Twenty-six had come. He had done this arithmetic twice already, and he did it again while pretending to listen to his uncle describe the property market, because the arithmetic was bothering him in a way he couldn't immediately name.

"Where's Rico?" Emilie asked, appearing beside him with a cup of the punch his mother had made too weak on purpose. "And that girl who used to sit behind you in Spanish. Ana? Anya?"

"Ayna," Landon said. "I don't know. I haven't talked to her since sophomore year."

"Right." Emilie looked out at the yard, where Jett was now losing to the twelve-year-old. "Weird how people just fall off."

Landon's mother had a framed photo from his ninth-grade orientation hanging in the hallway, forty-three kids in the gym in their lanyards, squinting into the flash. He had walked past it on his way to get more ice, and something about the photo had followed him back to the party like a dog. Forty-three. Twenty-six, minus the handful who had moved or had other parties tonight or simply hadn't wanted to come, still didn't feel like the same number as forty-three.

He found his phone and sat on the stairs, away from the music, and typed into it: US average adjusted cohort graduation rate. He read the result twice, then a third time, because the first two times it looked like something that couldn't apply to a gym with a water-stained ceiling. Eighty-seven percent in the 2021-22 school year, for public high school students. He said it quietly to himself, the whole phrase, adjusted cohort, as if the words might make it more personal or less.

"Are you hiding?" Emilie had followed him with the punch bowl, which was nearly empty and needed the kitchen anyway.

"Eighty-seven percent," he said. "The US average adjusted cohort graduation rate. Public high school students, 2021-22." He showed her the screen. "So thirteen out of every hundred don't finish. Or more, some years, some places. But that's the average."

Emilie set the bowl down on the banister and took the phone. "Where'd you find this?"

"Just now. It's federal data, I think. It's not about our school specifically." He was careful about that part, because he could already feel himself wanting the number to be a verdict, and it wasn't one, or at least not the verdict he wanted. "We had forty-three in that hallway photo. Eighty-seven percent of forty-three is thirty-seven and a half. So if we were exactly average, five or six of them aren't walking across a stage anywhere this month."

"Ayna," Emilie said. "Rico. DeShawn, the one who went to live with his grandma." She counted on the punch-sticky fingers of one hand and stopped at three, and then she didn't add any more names, and neither did he.

"It's not a bad number," Landon said. "It's actually, I don't know. I used to think it meant everybody makes it if they try. And then I used to think the opposite, that everyone's getting failed by everything. It's not really either. Eighty-seven out of a hundred is a lot of people in caps and gowns. And thirteen is a lot of empty chairs."

"So which is it?" Emilie asked. She had a way of asking questions that sounded like she already knew he didn't have an answer, and was asking anyway, out of interest.

"Both, I think. And I can't tell how much of the thirteen is about the chairs and how much is about something the chairs can't measure." He heard how that sounded, like something a person says on stairs at a party to sound like a person who says things on stairs. "I'm not sure I'll get a better answer than that."

Emilie picked up the bowl. "Your mom wants more ice."

In the kitchen, his mother was wiping down the counter with a dish towel that said LAKE HOUSE 2011, a lie in two words since they had never had one. He got the ice from the freezer, and his uncle called from the yard that Jett had lost twice more, and the tectonic arithmetic he'd been carrying around all evening settled into something quieter, still unresolved, present the way weather is present. He carried the tray of cubes out through the screen door, and Jett raised his cup toward him across the whole noisy yard and shouted, "To the eighty-seven percent."

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: Mexico's Day of the Dead is traditionally celebrated on November 1 and 2, when families build ofrendas, or home altars, with photos and the favorite foods and drinks of relatives who have died.
story:
Mya set the loaf of pan dulce on the kitchen table still warm from the bakery bag, its crust split like a small risen moon, and looked at the cleared corner by the window where her mother wanted the altar to go. Her grandmother had died in March, between one ordinary week and the next, and now it was late October and the house was finally ready to talk about it. Her mother had said only, "We build it together, whatever it is," and then gone to the store for candles, leaving Mya alone with the bread and the photographs.

Lena had told her about it first, weeks ago, sitting on the bleachers with their shoes touching. "November first and second," Lena had said, tracing the date on the fogged metal with her finger. "Day of the Dead. My abuela builds an ofrenda every year, a home altar, with photos and the person's favorite foods and drinks. My tio gets his tequila and his chicharrones. It's not sad, it's more like a visit." Mya had nodded the way you nod at someone else's tradition, filing it away, not guessing she would need it so soon.

Because the wanting had started before that, really. All summer she had wanted some way to say goodbye that the funeral hadn't provided. The funeral had been efficient, the pastor brisk, the aunts tearful and slightly bellicose about the seating chart, and Mya had stood at the graveside feeling like a guest at someone else's grief. Her grandmother had raised her half the time, had taught her to roll tortillas with a patience Mya never inherited, and Mya had repaid that by skipping her last two visits, in February, because of a track meet and a boy named in her phone only as D. She had told herself the visits would resume. This was the debt she carried now, and no ceremony she knew of accepted it as payment.

So when her mother came home with candles and sugar and a stack of photographs, Mya was the one who said, "Lena told me about the ofrenda. The bread goes first. It was her favorite." Her mother paused in the doorway, a bag in each hand, and something in her face shifted, not quite permission and not quite surprise, closer to relief that one of them knew where to begin.

They built it on the counter by the window, where the morning light came in. Mya arranged the photographs: her grandmother at forty in a floral dress, her grandmother old and laughing at a stove, her grandmother holding baby Mya like a loaf she was proud of. Her mother set out candles and a glass of water, then opened the pantry and stood there a long time. "I don't know what she drank," she said finally. "I know she liked coffee, but at night?"

"She liked horchata," Mya said, and heard herself say it with a confidence that surprised her, because she had watched the woman spoon rice into a blender a hundred times and never once asked what it was called. She made it that afternoon, badly, the rice gritty at the bottom of the glass, and put it on the altar anyway.

Milla came over around six, drawn by the smell of cinnamon, and stood at the edge of the kitchen with her coat still on. "Is this the Mexican thing?" she asked, and Mya felt a small defensive flare, the urge to vilify the question as careless, and let it pass, because Milla's face was open and her grandmother had died two springs ago with nothing built anywhere for her. "November first and second," Mya said. "Families make these home altars, ofrendas, with photos and the favorite foods and drinks of people who died. It's for visiting them." Milla looked at the horchata for a while. "My grandma liked lemon drops," she said. "I still have the tin."

Later, after Milla left with the tin promising to return, after her mother went to bed, Mya sat alone at the table with the last piece of pan dulce, and it seemed to her, though she distrusted the thought, like synchronicity: Lena mentioning the dates in October without knowing March was coming, the bakery two blocks over stocking the exact bread her grandmother had made, the way the tradition held both the living and the dead at one table as if the arrangement were obvious. She did not know whether the dead could visit, whether anything crossed the candlelight except moths. What she knew was that she had skipped two visits and could not skip this one, and that wanting to make the altar was not the same as deserving it, and that she had made it anyway.

The bread was sweet and a little dry, like the ones her grandmother used to buy when she was too tired to bake. Mya ate it slowly, facing the photographs, and when she reached the gritty bottom of the horchata she thought, next year I'll soak the rice longer, and she carried the glass to the sink and washed it by hand.

activity: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
knowledge_domain: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
fact: Josef Albers made over 1,000 works in his Homage to the Square series from 1950 until 1976, keeping nested squares constant while changing only the colours.
story:
Marcus had counted the squares in the painting twice, the way he counted the pills his father took each morning, as though counting could keep something steady. Four nested squares, the same in every frame along the wall, only the colours shifting from canvas to canvas like weather moving over one fixed field. He copied the wall label into his phone: Homage to the Square. Then the smaller print, which he read twice.

Over a thousand of these, the label said. Josef Albers made over 1,000 works in the series from 1950 until 1976, keeping the nested squares constant while changing only the colours. Twenty-six years, Marcus thought, doing arithmetic he didn't need to do. The man had made the same painting a thousand times and each one was different.

"That's the one Kara wouldn't shut up about," Remi said, appearing beside him with his jacket still on, though they'd been inside the small university gallery for half an hour. "She said it was lazy. Same composition every time."

"She said that?"

"At lunch. On Tuesday. You were at the dentist."

Marcus looked at the painting again, an orange centre going outward into reds that turned bruised and quiet at the edges. Last Tuesday he had been in a chair with his mouth open, thinking about the portfolio application due in December, ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement, and the theme was the thing he didn't have. He'd been maligning the whole assignment for weeks, calling it a cage, a factory, a trick to make seventeen-year-olds pretend to have unified souls. His sketchbook held thirty fragments of thirty ideas, none of which spoke to any other.

"Lazy," he said now, slowly, testing the word.

"Her word. You could fight her about it. You'd lose, but you could."

Mr. Balogun, who taught studio art and had driven three of them here in his dented hatchback, drifted past with his hands clasped behind his back and said nothing, which was his way of saying everything. Marcus followed the series down the wall instead, frame by frame, and the flashback arrived without being invited: he was nine, at his grandmother's apartment the summer before she moved to the home, and she was showing him how she made the same soup every Sunday, the same pot, the same order of ingredients, and when he asked if she ever got bored she said, "You don't understand. It's never the same soup. The tomatoes are different every week." He had thought this was a truism, something old people said to make repetition sound wise. He had thought that for seven years.

He stood in front of a panel where the same four squares went pale green into grey into a violet so cold it looked like an apology, and he understood that the constraint wasn't a cage at all. If the composition never moved, then colour had to carry everything, every mood, every argument, and the viewer would feel the difference precisely because nothing else changed. It was almost parsimonious, one variable and no more, like a science experiment his biology teacher would have approved of. Kara called it lazy. Albers had called it, presumably, twenty-six years of work.

"It's the opposite of lazy," Marcus said. "It's harder. You can't hide behind a new composition every time. You have to get everything out of one thing."

Remi tilted his head at the nearest canvas. "So what's your theme, then. For the portfolio."

Marcus had already begun to see it: ten paintings, the same house, his grandmother's house, the same angle, the same window with the same curtains, and in each one only the light changed. Morning, storm, late afternoon in November, the blue of a hospital corridor bleeding in through the glass. The statement would almost write itself, though he knew, standing there, that it wouldn't, that Kara would have questions, that the teacher reviewing the application would have questions, that his father might look at ten paintings of a house that had to be sold and say nothing in a way that said everything.

"The same composition ten times," he said. "Different colour each time. The light."

"Copycat," Remi said, but he said it looking at the wall, and his voice had gone thoughtful.

"Maybe," Marcus said, because it was true and it wasn't. He photographed the wall label, then the orange painting, then a corner of the green one where the grey met the violet, and Mr. Balogun paused behind them at the exit, keys already in his hand, waiting with the patience of a man who knew that what a student took from a gallery could not be chaperoned home.

"Two minutes," Marcus said, and turned back once more to the orange square, its centre burning quietly inside the bruised red, the same painting as a thousand others and nothing like any of them.

activity: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
knowledge_domain: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
fact: If people trust a central bank to keep inflation low, they ask for smaller wage and price increases, and that expectation itself helps keep inflation down.
story:
Paige sat at the kitchen table with her economics notes exhumed from the bottom of her backpack, four days crumpled and coffee-ringed from her mother's cup, and read the assignment line again: explain, in your own words, how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation. She had copied two diagrams from the textbook, both of which showed arrows converging on a box labeled "demand," and neither of which she could say out loud without feeling like a fraud. Ms. Greco had told them on the first day of the unit that anyone can memorize a diagram, and Paige had believed her, which was the problem.

The doorbell rang twice, the way Keaton always rang it, and then Cristiano let himself in through the back because he had never once used the front door of her house. They were carrying a bag of sugar, a sleeve of paper cups, and a folded card table, because on Saturday they were setting up a lemonade stand at the end of the street for the neighborhood yard sale. They spread everything across the counter and started arguing before Paige could hide her notes.

"Two dollars a cup," Keaton said. "Easy. Because sugar's going to cost more next month, everybody's saying so, so we should get ahead of it. Charge what the future costs, not what today costs." Cristiano shook his head and said that was exactly backwards, that if they priced for a future that hadn't happened, they'd be the ones making it happen, though he couldn't say how. Paige, measuring sugar into a pitcher, felt the argument snag on something in her notes.

"Wait," she said. "Say that part again. The part about charging for the future." Keaton repeated it, more stubbornly this time, and Cristiano rolled his eyes, and Paige pulled her crumpled notes out from under the card table and smoothed them flat beside the lemonade. The paragraph she'd skipped past three times was suddenly not boring. It said that people's expectations about inflation shaped what they asked for, that what everyone believed about next month changed what everyone charged this month.

"Okay, so think about it with the stand," she said, talking faster now, testing it as she went because she was still not sure she had it right. "If you expect everything to cost more next month, you raise your price today. And if the people buying expect it too, they ask for bigger wages to keep up. Everybody asking for more is part of what makes prices climb. But the reverse works too. If people trust the central bank to keep inflation low, they ask for smaller wage and price increases. And that expectation itself helps keep inflation down. Not the interest rate alone, the trusting. The rate hike kind of proves the bank is serious, and then people stop pricing in a worse future."

"So it's a disincentive," Cristiano said slowly. "Raising rates makes borrowing cost more, and that's a disincentive to spend, but the real trick is that it convinces everyone." Keaton said that sounded like magic, that you couldn't run an economy on vibes, and Paige said she wasn't sure vibes and policy were as separate as he thought, though she admitted the textbook didn't put it that way and neither, probably, should she on Monday. That was the part she flagged with a pencil: what she couldn't yet defend.

They mixed a test batch and carried three cups out to the porch, where Ms. Greco was walking her dog past the fence. She stopped, complimented the lemonade, and asked what they were arguing about. Keaton gave the trenchant version, that Paige thought a central bank could slow inflation mostly by being trustworthy, and he thought that was soft. Ms. Greco laughed and said she had owned the rental next door for eleven years, and she hadn't raised the rent this year, first time ever, because she'd watched the news and decided prices would settle back down.

"See," Paige said, and then caught herself, because one landlady was not a central bank and a street was not an economy, and she said so, and Cristiano said that was the most annoying and most impressive thing about her. On Saturday they set up the table at the end of the street, and Keaton taped the price sign to the front: one dollar a cup. "Because we expect things to be fine," he announced to the first customer, and Paige, pouring, said, "Don't oversell it."

activity: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
knowledge_domain: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
fact: Skimming means reading quickly for the general idea, while scanning means searching a text for one specific detail such as a name or number.
story:
The newspaper arrived with the injera, folded to its fourth page and smelling faintly of the kitchen's berbere. Maya had asked Mr. Bekele for it in what she hoped was a polite construction, and he had answered in Amharic, quick and warm, so that she caught only the word for "tomorrow" and had to guess the rest was permission.

She spread the paper across the corner table of his restaurant, where she came every Thursday after her shift bussing tables ended. In seven days she had to stand up in front of her Saturday class, read a short article in Amharic aloud, and summarize it in her own words. Her teacher had given her a photocopy of a piece about a river festival in a town whose name she could not yet pronounce. Three short paragraphs. She had been staring at the first one for eleven minutes, working word by word, looking up each unfamiliar term in her dictionary, writing translations in the margin until the margin ran out and the words crowded up against the print like rush-hour passengers.

Cecilia slid into the booth across from her, balancing a plate of leftover doro wat the cook had set aside for them. "You look like the newspaper insulted you."

"It sort of did." Maya turned the photocopied page around. "Every word I don't know, I look up. Then I forget the sentence by the time I get to the end of it."

Cecilia squinted at the page. "What do you actually need to find first? You said the summary is due, not a translation."

"The date of the festival. The teacher wants us to state when it happens before anything else." Maya's finger was already traveling down the page, halting at every second word, decoding, decoding.

"You're doing it the slow way." Cecilia leaned over and tapped the article. "Just hunt for the date. Like when you look for your own name in a group photo."

"That's not the same thing."

"It is. That's called scanning. You're going through the text for one specific thing, a name or a number. Skimming is different, that's reading quickly for the general idea." Cecilia said it the way she said everything, flat and certain, as if she were reading a weather report. Then she went back to her chicken.

Maya sat with that for a moment. She had spent weeks assuming that reading in a new language meant reading every word, that anything less was cheating, a shortcut that would leave holes in her understanding. But the holes were already there; they were just arriving more slowly and with more exhaustion. She set the dictionary facedown on the seat beside her, put her finger at the top of the first paragraph, and moved her eyes down the lines without stopping, letting the letter shapes pass by until one shape snagged: a cluster she recognized, the numerals for the ninth month embedded in the Amharic line. There. The festival fell in September. It had taken eleven seconds.

"Found it," she said, and something in her chest loosened like a knot worked free with a thumb.

She tried the next task differently too. Instead of translating the second paragraph line by line, she skimmed it, fast, twice, letting the words she knew carry her and the words she didn't slide past like unfamiliar buildings on a street she was learning. The paragraph was about preparations, she could tell that much; boats, she thought, or maybe baskets, and she honestly could not say which, and she noticed that the uncertainty did not frighten her the way it had an hour ago. She had assumed comprehension arrived all at once or not at all. Maybe it arrived in layers, the way the restaurant's smells did, first the coffee, then the cardamom under it, then something she would only identify later when Mr. Bekele told her its name.

He came over to refill her water and glanced at the newspaper. "You read this fast now," he said in English, teasing.

"Not fast. Just differently. I was reading like a translator before. Now I'm reading like a reader." She paused. "Sort of. A slow reader."

Cayden arrived at six, damp from the rain outside, and pulled a chair up to the end of the booth. He had started the same Saturday class a term ahead of her, and when she told him about the article, he pulled out his phone and showed her the app he used, which grouped words by their dictionary forms, each entry a lemma with its relatives gathered under it, so that if she knew the root for "gather," she could meet "gathering" and "they gathered" as cousins rather than strangers. She copied the name of the app onto her wrist in pen. It felt less like memorizing and more like being introduced to a family, and she wondered whether that was what fluency actually was, not knowing more words but knowing fewer of them as strangers.

By closing time she had a summary drafted on a napkin: a river festival in September, preparations involving boats or baskets, an official quoted about a change she could not pin down. Two of the three points she could defend. The third she marked with a small question mark, and when Mr. Bekele came to wipe the table, she asked him, in Amharic, whether the word she had guessed meant "bother" or "delay." He shook his head, amused, and said it meant the river itself had been dredged, and she wrote "dredged" in English above the word and underlined nothing, letting the correction sit there unhidden.

The next Thursday she came back with her graded summary in her bag, a B plus with a note about strong main ideas and shaky detail. She ordered the same table, the same corner, and asked Mr. Bekele for the newspaper again, in the polite construction she had now used enough times to internalize, the words coming out shaped right without her checking them first. He brought it folded to a different page and stood there while she opened it.

"New article," he said. "Harder one."

She looked at the dense columns, at the headline she could only half decode, and found that her first instinct was no longer to reach for a dictionary. She was already scanning the page, hunting for a date, a name, anything with a handle on it.

"All right," she said. "Boats or baskets."

activity: ethical questions raised by technology such as algorithmic bias, surveillance and automation
knowledge_domain: ethical questions raised by technology such as algorithmic bias, surveillance and automation
fact: A 2013 study by Carl Benedikt Frey and Michael Osborne estimated that 47 percent of US jobs were at high risk of automation.
story:
The message arrived at 9:47 on a Tuesday, while Jasmine was still rinsing out the coffee urn at Gilbert's Market: "they're putting in the machines saturday." It came from Etienne, who had the closing shift and a habit of texting the group chat things he'd overheard but never asked about directly. Roxanne answered within a minute with a row of exclamation points, and then, "which machines." Jasmine dried her hands, took her phone into the stockroom where the light was better, and typed, "self-checkout. four of them. they were in boxes by the loading dock since monday."

She had applied to Gilbert's because her mother had said a job would teach her something, and so far it had taught her the smell of wet cardboard and the exact sound a receipt printer makes before it jams. She worked Saturdays and two evenings after school, scanning groceries, mostly for people who did not look at her. The owner had never mentioned machines. Neither had the schedule, which had been posted every Sunday for as long as anyone could remember, though lately it had changed. Jasmine's hours had thinned from nineteen a week to eleven, and when she'd asked, the owner had shown her a spreadsheet on his laptop and said the system did the scheduling now, based on demand modeling. He said it like the matter was closed, and she supposed it was, though she noticed that Roxanne, who worked the same shifts, still had nineteen.

In the group chat that night, Roxanne was indignant about the machines on principle. "they're just going to make us bag our own stuff and accuse us of stealing," she wrote, and Etienne replied, "my dad says they call it automation," which was the first time Jasmine had seen the word written out, though she'd heard the owner use it on the phone once, apologetically, as if explaining a doctor's verdict. She looked it up in bed with her phone brightness turned low, and the search led her somewhere she hadn't expected: a study from 2013, by two researchers named Carl Benedikt Frey and Michael Osborne, estimating that 47 percent of US jobs were at high risk of automation. She read the number twice. It was old, older than her little brother, and it still felt like a hand pressing lightly on the back of her neck.

She sent the link to the chat. "47 percent," she typed, and then, because she didn't want it to seem like a warning, "of US jobs. at high risk. from a 2013 study." Roxanne responded with a skull emoji and the word "cheerful." Etienne said nothing for a while, and then: "does the study say anything about high school students." It didn't, or if it did, Jasmine couldn't find it, and she told him so honestly. What she kept to herself was a smaller observation she couldn't shake: the self-checkout machines wouldn't replace her exactly. There would still be someone watching them, one person orbiting four machines instead of three people at three registers, and the person the scheduling software kept at nineteen hours was not the person whose family had two incomes.

She tested the thought out loud on Saturday, when Mr. Cho from next door came through her line with his usual contrivance of coupons, each one clipped and sorted and presented with ceremony, as if the register were an opponent to be outmaneuvered. "You'll be gone soon," he said pleasantly, nodding at the plastic-wrapped machines being unwheeled past the entrance. "Not yet," Jasmine said. "They still need somebody to watch them." Mr. Cho considered this while she extruded the receipt from a printer that had chosen that moment to jam. "Somebody to watch," he repeated. "When I was young, somebody watched the elevator. Then the elevator learned to watch itself."

That evening the owner called her. She assumed it was about Saturday's till, which had been off by a dollar forty, but he wanted to ask whether she'd be interested in a new position: attendant for the self-checkout area, more hours, slightly better pay. "The system flags you as reliable," he said. "Low error rate, good customer ratings." Jasmine stood in her kitchen holding the phone, and after he hung up she opened the group chat, typed a message to Etienne and Roxanne, deleted it, and typed a different one. "got offered the machine job," she wrote. "more money." Roxanne answered fast: "so you'd be the one the machines replaced us with." It wasn't cruel, the way she said it, but it wasn't not cruel either.

Jasmine sat with the phone in her lap and looked out at the porch light, where a moth kept at the bulb with a persistence that was either devotion or failure to learn. She thought about telling Mr. Cho, who would probably say something tidy about elevators. She thought about the scheduling software, which had never met her and had somehow decided she was reliable, and whether being flattered by a system she couldn't inspect was different from being dismissed by it. Both felt like weather: real, consequential, not addressed to her personally. She picked the phone back up and started typing. "i haven't said yes yet," she wrote. "can we talk about it at lunch tomorrow, all three of us, in person."

activity: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
knowledge_domain: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
fact: Consent to sexual activity must be freely given and can be withdrawn at any time, including after activity has already started.
story:
The waiting room of the Riverside Clinic smelled like hand sanitizer and old magazines, and Jordan had been rehearsing under his breath for twenty minutes, which was why Zahra finally took the flashcards out of his hands.

"You're externalizing again," she said. "Saying everything out loud so the whole room can hear you panic."

"I'm not panicking. I'm studying." He took the cards back. "Braylon asked me to do this. He won't come himself. He says clinics are for people who have something wrong with them."

Zahra raised an eyebrow at that, and Jordan let it go, because they both knew the real reason was more complicated than Braylon would admit. His friend had a girlfriend now, an older girlfriend, and had cornered Jordan after practice with a question he'd practically whispered: so what do you actually do, before any of it, so nothing goes wrong? Jordan had said he'd find out, and then had realized he didn't know either. Their health unit in the spring had been four days of Ms. Chan diagraming things on the whiteboard while the class snickered, and Jordan had snickered too, which meant he'd absorbed almost nothing. Hence the flashcards Zahra made, hence the appointment he'd booked for his sports physical, with a private list of questions folded in his sock like contraband.

"Okay, role-play," Zahra said, dropping into the chair beside him. "I'm a patient. You're the counselor. I'll ask what people actually ask."

"Fine."

"What's contraception, and where do I get it?"

"Condoms, the pill, IUDs, other stuff. Condoms are at the drugstore, no age requirement. The pill and everything else you get here, or at Planned Parenthood, and you don't need a parent's permission in this state." He said it fast, like stepping over ice.

"Good. What if I want to get tested for infections?"

"You can walk in or call. They test urine and blood, sometimes a swab. Some results in a few days. It's confidential, they mail nothing home, they call your cell."
