He'd checked that part twice, because Braylon's father opened all the mail at their house, a fact Braylon had mentioned once and never repeated.

Zahra shuffled the cards, then looked up with a different face on, the face she used when a question was real. "Last one, and this one's mine, not the cards. If someone says yes to something, and then in the middle of it they change their mind. Are they allowed?"

The waiting room went on around them, a toddler stacking blocks, a TV murmuring the weather. Jordan had an answer on the tip of his tongue and then hesitated, because the answer mattered and he could feel it mattering. "Yes," he said. "Consent has to be freely given, and the person can withdraw it at any time. Even after it's already started."

"So they say stop, and the other person has to stop."

"That's the whole thing. That's what makes it consent." He heard how thin his voice got on the last word, not from doubt but from the weight of saying it out loud in a public room, and Zahra nodded once, slow, like she was filing it somewhere.

When the nurse called his name, Jordan followed her down the hallway and got weighed and measured and told to wait in the second exam room, where Ms. Chan, it turned out, was covering the practice that afternoon. She was grayer than he remembered from school but the same brisk way of flipping open a folder. He sat on the crinkling paper of the exam table and pulled the folded list out of his sock.

"I have questions that aren't about my physical," he said. "For a friend. Mostly."

Ms. Chan read the list, and for a moment he thought she was going to laugh, but she didn't. She went through it line by line, drew him a map of the clinic's testing hours, slid two pamphlets across the counter, and said that if the friend wanted, he could book under the same last name as a hundred other kids in this city and no one would blink. Then she paused at the third question, the one Zahra had asked in the waiting room, the one Jordan had written out and then rewritten trying to get it right.

"This one you already have the answer to," she said. "It's written correctly. Freely given, withdrawn at any time, including after the start." She handed the paper back. "The hard part isn't knowing it. The hard part is saying it to someone when it's awkward."

Outside, in the parking lot, Jordan texted Braylon a photo of the pamphlets side by side on the hood of a car, the clinic's number circled in pen. He typed and deleted three explanations, profligate with words he didn't need, and finally sent only: Tuesday walk-ins until six. I'll go with you if you want. Not a lecture, not a paragraph about being careful. Just the door, held open. The reply came back as a single thumbs-up, then, thirty seconds later, a second message: what do I say when I get there. Jordan smiled and started typing, you just tell them you want to get tested, and let me tell you about the form.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: In 2018 economists Joshua Miller and Adam Sanjurjo showed the 1985 hot-hand analysis had a statistical bias and found evidence of streak shooting in the same data.
story:
The gym smelled of rubber and cold coffee by the time Florence got there, half an hour early as she had done every Tuesday since November. She liked the emptiness, the way her footsteps doubled off the far wall, the chance to shoot without anyone keeping count of her misses. Mr. Chowdhury was already at the scoring table with his clipboard, arranging cones, and he raised two fingers at her without looking up, which meant he wanted her on layups first, then free throws, and that he had noticed she had made only four of her last ten from the line.

She was on her seventeenth shot when Aikam pushed through the double doors with his laptop bag over one shoulder and his sneakers already tied. He had quit the team in grade ten and come back this season as something between manager and menace, sitting on the bench with a spreadsheet open, logging every attempt. "You're at eleven of seventeen," he said, dropping onto the floor to stretch. "Which is above your average, but I need a bigger sample before I say you're hot."

"Aikam." Mr. Chowdhury's voice carried the length of the court without being loud. "How many times."

"It's not superstition, it's a question." Aikam stood and walked to the table, unhurried, because this argument was an old one and they both took a certain comfort in it. "Everyone talks about the hot hand. The players believe it. You believe it. In 1985 a famous study looked for streak shooting and said it wasn't real, just people seeing patterns in noise."

"And?" Mr. Chowdhury set down a cone.

"And in 2018, two economists, Joshua Miller and Adam Sanjurjo, showed the 1985 hot-hand analysis had a statistical bias, and they found evidence of streak shooting in the same data." Aikam said it evenly, the way he said most things, as if he were handing over a receipt. "The same data. What everyone thought proved there was nothing actually proved the opposite, once you fixed the flaw."

Florence had stopped shooting to listen. She knew the shape of the disagreement by now: Mr. Chowdhury had played semi-pro in Dhaka before anyone kept spreadsheets, and he ran practices on feel, on the set of a guard's shoulders, on a hunch about who should take the last shot. Aikam wanted to predicate every decision on numbers, and when the numbers and the coach disagreed, he treated the disagreement as an error to be corrected rather than a fact about the world.

The rest of the team arrived in a clatter, Judy last as always, hair still wet, mouthing sorry at Florence across the court. Florence passed her the ball so she could join the layup line without standing alone at the end of it, and Judy's shoulder bumped hers in thanks.

The problem arrived in the third quarter of the Thursday game, though it had been assembling itself all season. Florence had missed her first five shots, and Mr. Chowdhury had left her in anyway, which Aikam later said was indefensible, a profligate use of minutes when the bench was deeper than the schedule. Then she hit two in a row, then a third, and the crowd began that low murmuring sound, and Mr. Chowdhury called a set play for her that had not been run once all year. She made it. On the bench afterward, toweling off, she heard Aikam say quietly, "That's four of her last six," and Judy said, "Told you she was hot," and the two of them looked at each other with the particular wariness of people who believe in different physics.

Afterward, in the emptying change room, Florence sat unlacing her shoes and tried to hold both versions in her head at once. If Aikam was right that streaks were real, then Mr. Chowdhury's instinct was not superstition but something the coach had been reading correctly all along without being able to say how. But if she was honest, and she tried to be, she could not always tell the difference between being hot and merely remembering her makes more vividly than her misses. Yesterday in math they had argued about relativism, some boy insisting that every opinion was equally valid, and she had hated the argument, and yet here she was wanting to say the coach and the spreadsheet were both right, which felt dangerously close to the same laziness.

She found Aikam waiting by the doors, laptop under his arm, breath fogging in the cold. "Can I ask you something," she said. "That study. If the fix showed streaks were real, then what the coach does isn't wrong. He just can't prove it."

"It's not proof, it's evidence," Aikam said. "Different thing. And it's evidence about players on average. It doesn't tell me tonight's version of you will make the next one." He shifted the laptop to his other arm. "It tells me it's worth betting on, sometimes."

"And you'd still bench me when I start cold."

"I'd bench you when the numbers say to. He wouldn't." Aikam looked back at the gym doors. "One of us loses more games. I'm just not sure which one."

Florence laughed, and the sound surprised her, and he almost smiled. Inside, the lights were going out one bank at a time, and through the narrow window in the door she could see Mr. Chowdhury standing at half court in the half dark, rolling a ball along the floor to no one, the way he always did after games, win or lose. She pushed the door open and walked back onto the court, and he passed her the ball without a word.

activity: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
knowledge_domain: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
fact: Test-driven development, popularized by Kent Beck, follows a 'red, green, refactor' cycle: write a failing test, make it pass, then clean up the code.
story:
The lab was too cold for July, and Sarah had been staring at the same blank file for ten minutes. On the whiteboard, Ms. Bianchi had written the assignment in her dour, upright hand: a Student class in Java, with private fields and getter methods, and it had to pass a test suite the students wrote themselves. Not afterward. First.

"First how?" Logan whispered across the aisle. "There's nothing to test. The class doesn't exist."

Sarah scrolled the spec sheet again. At the bottom, in smaller print, a line she'd skimmed past: write your test before you write the class. Below it, a name she didn't recognize, Kent Beck, and three words in quotes. "What's red, green, refactor?" she whispered back.

"No idea."

Ms. Bianchi walked the rows like a proctor at an exam, answering nothing. When Sarah raised her hand and asked whether the test could come second, just this once, Ms. Bianchi said only, "Try it the way it's written," and moved on.

Sarah wrote the test anyway, feeling absurd. getName on an object she couldn't yet construct, assertEquals where assertEquals could never pass, because there was no class to compile against. The editor flagged everything red. Then she understood the first word, or thought she did: red was this, the failing test, the error she was supposed to want. She built a bare Student class, added a private field called name, wrote a getter, and ran the test. Green. It was almost disappointing how quickly it came.

"It's a trick," Logan said, leaning over. "You pass the test, you're done."

"No, there's a third part." Sarah was rereading the board. Refactor. She had heard the word once from her uncle, who used shop talk the way other people used a vernacular to shut strangers out, and she'd assumed it meant renovation. Here it seemed to mean something smaller: clean up the code without changing what it did. Her getter worked but it was ugly, the field initialized in two places, a stray print statement left over from panicking. She deleted the prints, consolidated the initialization, ran the test again. Still green.

Paxton, two seats down, was watching them. "So Beck's whole idea is you go around the loop every time? Failing test, passing test, cleanup. Every single feature."

"Seems like it," Sarah said. "You write the test, watch it fail, make it pass, then refactor." She said it plainly, testing the shape of it against what she'd just done, and it fit. Paxton wrote it in the margin of her notebook like something she intended to argue with later.

What Sarah couldn't decide, walking to the bus with her laptop heavy in her bag, was whether the discipline was honest or just ritual. Her old habits, inculcated through three years of getting programs working by any means and cleaning up only if a teacher looked, had produced code that passed and code that lied. This way the test failed out loud before anything pretended otherwise. But she could see the other side too: Paxton's margin note, the suspicion that a rule followed blindly was only a different kind of blindness. Ms. Bianchi hadn't explained any of it, which Sarah was beginning to think was the point.

At home she opened the file again and added a second test, for a field she hadn't built yet, and watched the editor turn red.

"Sarah," her mother called from the kitchen, "dinner."

"Two minutes."

She ran it once more, the failure blooming down the console, and started typing.

fact: A 1985 study by Gilovich, Vallone and Tversky called basketball's 'hot hand' an illusion, but a 2018 reanalysis by Miller and Sanjurjo found a statistical flaw and evidence of streak shooting.
story:
Nevaeh had claimed the good folding chair at Ms. Baptiste's house an hour before tipoff, which mattered because the chair was the only seat with a clear line to the television that didn't require looking past somebody's elbow. Around her, the living room filled: her father with his paper plate of wings, Princess with a bowl of popcorn she refused to share, and Ms. Baptiste's nephew DeAndre, who had money on the game and said so twice.

The Hornets were down nine at the half, and then their guard, Marcos Webb, scored on four straight possessions. A three from the corner, a layup through traffic, another three, a pull-up jumper. DeAndre stood up. "That's it. He's hot. He's going for forty tonight."

"He's not hot," Princess said. "It's just random. People miss three, make three, and everybody invents a pattern." Princess wanted to be right more than she wanted anything else in that room; she'd spent a whole semester of lunch periods correcting people's grammar and hadn't stopped since. She had also, Nevaeh knew, written a paper on this exact question.

"They studied it," Princess went on. "Nineteen eighty-five. Gilovich, Vallone and Tversavy, whatever. They called it the hot hand and said it's an illusion."

"Gilovich, Vallone and Tversky," Nevaeh said. "And that's not the end of it."

Princess turned in her seat. "You're going to prevaricate now? You agreed with me in October."

"I'm not prevaricating. I changed my mind, which is different." Nevaeh had changed it in the fall, during the unit Ms. Baptiste taught on probability. Ms. Baptiste had put the 1985 study on the projector and let the class tear at it for two days, and on the second day she'd slid a printout across Nevaeh's desk without comment. The printout was the 2018 reanalysis, Miller and Sanjurjo, and Nevaeh had read it that night at her kitchen table with her mother watching her show in the background, and had sat there feeling as though the floor had tilted a few degrees. The old study had a statistical flaw, the reanalysis said. There was evidence of streak shooting.

"Fine," Princess said. "Explain it, then."

Nevaeh pointed at the screen instead of explaining, because Webb had just missed twice and DeAndre was already groaning. "See, that's the problem. One miss proves nothing either way. That's what I got wrong before. I thought believing in the hot hand was like, solipsism, just projecting your own story onto randomness. But the reanalysis found an actual flaw in how the original data was read. So the question isn't whether fans are silly. The question is whether the effect is real, and it might be."

Ms. Baptiste, folding towels in the doorway between the kitchen and the living room, said nothing. She never said anything during these arguments anymore, not since the day in class when she'd told them she was done handing out conclusions like graded papers.

DeAndre's vitriolic response to the referee's charging call on Webb drew a warning look from her, and he lowered his voice. "So which is it? Hot or not hot? You can't have it both ways."

"Why not? The evidence is conflicting, and I don't have to pick a side tonight."

"That's a cop-out."

"It's not a cop-out. It's what the evidence allows." Nevaeh's father, who had been silent through most of this, took another wing and said, "In my day we just called it rhythm." Nobody answered him.

Webb hit his next shot, a fadeaway from the elbow, and the room came up off its seats. DeAndre was pacing between the couch and the television with both hands on his head. Princess had gone quiet, watching the screen with her arms crossed, and Nevaeh understood that her friend wasn't arguing anymore, only watching to see whether the game itself would take a side, which it never did, which was the whole trouble.

The Hornets cut the lead to two with four minutes left. Webb touched the ball on the next possession, sized up his defender, and rose from twenty-four feet. Nevaeh leaned forward, and Princess, without looking away from the screen, said, "Don't you dare be right." The ball left his hand, hung there, and came down toward the rim with the whole room standing.

activity: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
knowledge_domain: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
fact: Stage directions in a script are usually set apart in italics or parentheses so actors and directors can tell them from spoken lines.
story:
The debate tournament shared its venue with a community theatre, which meant Eric spent his lunch break wedged between a rack of costumes and a folding table where Ms. Islam, the drama coach who had agreed to run a playwriting workshop between rounds, was handing out thick packets. He had signed up because Carson said it would look good on applications, and Carson had signed up because Eric had, and now neither of them could back out. Zane hadn't signed up at all but had followed them in and taken a packet anyway, sitting down as if the chair had been reserved for him.

"A ten-minute play," Ms. Islam said. "One moment from your own life. It can be small. Small is better."

Eric had prepared cases on sanctions and on whether the voting age should be lowered, arguments he could amortize across a whole season of tournaments, reusing the same evidence until the effort of assembling it had paid for itself many times over. A moment from his own life, though, could not be reused or spread out. It could only be shown once, badly or otherwise.

He wrote about the morning his father drove him to his first debate tournament and got lost twice and refused to admit it, and how they had sat in the parked car outside the school for a full minute not saying anything, and how Eric had finally said the thing about the GPS that made his father laugh. It took him most of the hour. At the bottom of the page, where the characters did things, he wrote those things in ordinary sentences among the dialogue, because that was how it had occurred to him.

Ms. Islam gathered them into the theatre's green room for a read-through, the kind with mismatched chairs and a kettle nobody trusted. She cast herself as the father, Zane as Eric, and Carson as the GPS, which Carson declared was the role he was born for. They began. Zane read Eric's lines, Ms. Islam read the father's, and then, three lines in, Ms. Islam read aloud, in a perfectly serious parental voice, "He checks his phone, embarrassed."

Silence. Zane started laughing first, a wheeze that folded him over the packet. "Why did you say that part?"

"That part is a stage direction," Ms. Islam said, still in character, which made it worse. "In a script, stage directions are set apart in italics or in parentheses, so the actors and directors can tell them from the spoken lines." She tapped Eric's page. "Yours aren't set apart. They're hiding among the dialogue like civilians."

Carson, from inside his GPS voice, said, "Recalculating. Recalculating," and the room came apart again.

Eric felt the flush arrive, incipient at his ears and then everywhere, and then felt it turn into something else, something almost like the moment in cross-examination when an opponent's case opened a door you hadn't known existed. He had written the scene the way a debater writes, everything in one stream, all evidence and no staging. The distinction wasn't decoration. It was how a script told a director what to do with a body in a chair.

He borrowed a pen and went through the pages, circling every action, every pause, every check-of-the-phone, and marking them off in their own lane. Some he put in parentheses. Where the parenthetical got crowded he drew a line down the margin instead, an invented convention, and decided it was allowed, because the point was the separation, not the ceremony.

They read it again. This time Zane stopped at the directions instead of voicing them, and the strangest thing happened: the pauses did work. When Ms. Islam, as the father, sat in the parked car and said nothing for the length of two stage directions, Eric heard his own morning back, and it was better than the version with everything spoken. Carson's GPS remained, in his professional opinion, the emotional centerpiece.

"That's the one, though," Eric said afterward, pointing at a direction he could not fix with italics or parentheses: the father laughing. "I can put it in the stage directions but I can't make it happen. He either laughs or he doesn't."

"Welcome to the theatre," Ms. Islam said, stacking the chairs.

Zane argued the point all the way back to the debate room, insisting that if you wrote the laugh right, the actor had no choice, that the script was a kind of determinism with better lighting. Eric wasn't sure. He had watched his own father that morning, and the laugh had felt like a coin landing on its edge, no case, no warrant, no predictable outcome. He thought maybe a good play was the argument you made for the laugh and the honesty of admitting you could lose it.

His round was called. He picked up his debate file, and, without deciding to, the marked-up play, and carried both through the double doors.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: The 2018 World Cup in Russia was the first to use video assistant referees, who can review goals, penalties, direct red cards and cases of mistaken identity.
story:
The living room had filled by the second half: Nathaniel's father in the armchair, Jocelyn and Abygail shoulder to shoulder on the couch, Mr. Ivanova from next door perched on the ottoman with his elbows on his knees. On the screen, Russia 2018 had gone to its final minutes, and the score was even. When the ball hit the net off a corner, the room detonated, and then, as the referee touched his ear and stopped jogging, it went quiet in a different way, a held-breath quiet.

"VAR," Abygail said, and Nathaniel said it with her, the word already worn smooth from a whole tournament of saying it.

He had looked it up a month ago, after a group-stage match that ended with a penalty nobody in the room could account for. This was the first World Cup with video assistant referees, and they could review only certain things: goals, penalties, direct red cards, and cases of mistaken identity. Everything else, the pushing at corners, the shirt-tugging, the dissent, stayed beyond their reach. He had explained none of this at the time. He had just read it twice on his phone in the kitchen and come back in.

"What are they checking?" his father asked.

"The goal," Jocelyn said. "Offside, maybe, or a foul before it."

"They can't just check anything," Nathaniel said. "It's only four things. Goals, penalties, straight reds, and if they card the wrong player." He heard his own voice and worried it sounded like showing off, the way it had in September when he had corrected Mr. Ivanova about a handball rule and the old man had gone choleric, red to the ears, and left the barbecue early.

Mr. Ivanova turned on the ottoman. "You are certain of this."

"It's true. First time they've had it at all, this World Cup. That's why it keeps stopping like this."

The linesman had his flag down. The referee stood with his hand at his jaw, listening. On the replay, the scorer appeared level with the last defender, and then a drawn line appeared, slanting, and the scorer's shoulder was past it by a margin that seemed absurd, a toe's worth of offside. The room split at once. Abygail was on her feet calling it chicanery, an inch of a shoulder ruining a goal in the ninetieth minute. His father said the rule was the rule and had always been the rule; the cameras had merely cauterized the argument that used to bleed for decades. Jocelyn said nothing, watching the referee.

Nathaniel found that he agreed with both of them, or with parts of both, and could not make the parts into one thing. The decision was more accurate. That seemed undeniable. The line was drawn by a machine and the man was offside and the goal was dead, and in the old days they would have argued about it at this very gathering for years, replaying it from memory, each side certain. But accuracy was arriving like a bill. Something in the celebration had been amputated; the room had cheered and then had to wait, holding the cheer, unsure whether to keep it or put it away.

"Fine, it's right," Abygail said, dropping back onto the couch. "It's right and it's terrible. Both."

"Both," Nathaniel said, before he had decided to.

Mr. Ivanova grunted. He was a man who believed the game had been better when it was wrong more often, though he had never put it that way; he put it as "this is not football," and let the sentence stand in for a whole argument. Nathaniel had spent the tournament wanting to argue back. Now he was less sure which side he was on, and he noticed that the wanting had cooled into something more like attention.

The referee pointed to the center circle, then, after a beat, disallowed it. Free kick, the other way. Abygail made a sound like a kettle and Jocelyn pulled a cushion into her lap and hugged it. His father stood up to get more ice, which was what he did instead of swearing.

They watched the last two minutes in silence that was not quite peace. Nathaniel thought about how the machine had been right and everyone in the room had gone quiet anyway, and he could not tell whether the quiet was grief for the goal or something larger, and he was honest enough with himself to leave that question open. The final whistle came. Somebody had lost, somebody had won, and the room began collecting plates.

Mr. Ivanova stood, stretched, and looked at Nathaniel on his way to the door.

"Four things," he said. "You said four."

"Goals, penalties, reds, wrong man. Yes."

The old man nodded once, put on his coat, and paused with his hand on the latch. "Next tournament," he said, "they will find a fifth."

fact: Johann Maelzel patented the mechanical metronome in 1815, drawing on a design by Dietrich Nikolaus Winkel.
story:
The metronome had belonged to Christopher's grandfather, and it sat on the piano at home, a wooden pyramid with a brass pendulum that nobody wound anymore. He had asked his father who made it, and his father had said, "Johann Maelzel patented it in 1815," and then, halfway to the kitchen, "though the design was really Dietrich Winkel's. Maelzel took it." Christopher had repeated the names to himself at breakfast the next morning, the way he repeated fingering patterns, until they held.

In the band room on Tuesday, Ms. Yoon set the electric metronome on the stand beside him and clicked it to eighty. "Again. Sixteenth notes, two bars, then rest."

He played the two bars. His attack was late, a fraction, and he heard it.

"You're placing the note after the click," she said. "Listen first. Then play."

Down the row, Izabelle lowered her flute long enough to say, "You're scared of it."

"I'm not scared of it."

"You're waiting to see if it'll hurt you."

Rachel, from the percussion section, rolled a soft snare paradiddle without looking up. "He is. I've watched him. He flinches at the click."

He had no answer for that, so he played the two bars again, and again the notes came in behind, apologizing their way in.

That night he wound the grandfather's metronome for the first time. The pendulum swung with a dry, wooden tick, nothing like the electronic chirp at school, and he set the sliding weight where his father said sixty lived and played his scales against it. His grandfather had been a lawyer, a man his mother called sagacious in a tone that meant he had won arguments he should have lost. On the shelf above the piano there were still his casebooks, dense with annotations, and Christopher, resting between scales, opened one to see the margins crowded with his grandfather's cramped hand, every precedent transcribed in columns, authority stacked on authority, whole systems built out of what other men had decided first.

He closed the book and played, and this time he tried to land on the click instead of behind it, and something in the sound told him it was right, the way two things that are meant to coincide make one thing.

At Thursday's rehearsal he got there early and took the metronome off the stand before anyone could set it for him. Rachel watched him click it to ninety.

"Bold," she said.

"Grandpa's went slower."

"Grandpa had one?"

"Wooden. Maelzel patented it in 1815." He tucked the trumpet under his arm. "Based on Winkel's design. Winkel invented it first. Maelzel just got the patent."

"Sounds like theft."

"Sounds like jurisprudence," Izabelle said, arriving with her flute case and a granola bar. "Whoever files first."

Christopher set the metronome ticking and played the passage at ninety, and for eight bars he was with it, on it, not behind, and then the rest of the band trickled in and Ms. Yoon called them to their places and the moment passed.

Afterward she kept him a minute. "Better," she said. "You stopped apologizing."

"I was following Winkel," he said.

She looked at him without expression. "Whoever that is, keep following him."

At home he practiced against the wooden tick until his embouchure gave out, and then he sat with the casebook again, thinking about Maelzel taking the design, patenting it, putting his own name on a thing that already existed in someone else's hands. History had kept both names. His father knew both. But the patent office knew one, and the stores knew one, and probably most people who wound a metronome knew none.

He wasn't sure which side of that he was on when he played. The click was not his; the notes were; and the trick seemed to be meeting one with the other exactly, neither early like a thief arriving before the owner, nor late like someone asking permission. He could not have said whether that was true or only a thing that felt true, and he noticed he did not much care to decide.

On Saturday, Rachel texted: coming in to practice? doors open till four.

He packed the trumpet, then went back for the wooden metronome, wrapping it in a scarf inside his backpack, and rode the four miles to school with the weight of it against his spine.

She was already at the snare when he walked into the band room, and he set the pyramid on the edge of the timpani case and slid the weight up the pendulum.

"That's the real one," she said.

He wound the key. The tick filled the room.

"Ninety," he said, and lifted the horn.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: The first instant replay on television was shown by CBS during the Army-Navy football game on December 7, 1963, using a system devised by director Tony Verna.
story:
The cold in the stadium settled first into Jaxon's fingers and then into his judgment, which was why he kept his hands in his armpits and tried to think only about the game. He sat between his father and Mekhi, with Hugh two rows down beside a Navy midshipman who had been shouting since the opening kickoff. The stands were a single organism, swaying and groaning, and for three quarters Jaxon let it carry him along, captivated by the drum cadence and the flags and the way sixty thousand strangers could want one thing at the same time.

Then came the fumble. Or the non-fumble. The Navy returner took the ball at the twelve, got hit high, hit low, went down in a pile of gray and gold, and when the bodies were peeled apart the ball sat on the grass and an Army lineman was holding it over his head like a trophy. Half the stadium roared. The other half made a sound Jaxon had never heard before, low and aggrieved, the sound of a crowd refusing a version of events.

"That was down," Mekhi said, standing anyway, though the play was over and standing changed nothing. "His knee was down before it came out. Jaxon, you saw it."

"I saw a pile," Jaxon said. "I saw a pile and then a guy holding a ball."

Hugh turned around from the lower row, choleric in a way Jaxon had never seen from him, his face blotched red above his scarf. "Put it on the screen," he shouted, gesturing at the giant board hanging over the end zone, though the board showed only a rotating advertisement for a bank. "They have the cameras. They have all those cameras pointing at the field. Put the play on the screen!"

Jaxon's father leaned over and said, quietly, that the home team controlled the board, and the home team was not going to show the crowd sixty thousand reasons to throw hot chocolate onto the field. The referee announced something the wind ate half of, and the ruling on the field stood, and Army's offense came out.

Mekhi sat down hard. "It's not fair that we can't see it. There's a camera on every yard line. What's the point of the cameras?"

Jaxon had an answer, or the shape of one, and it surprised him that he had it. In the fall, for a history assignment on how television changed sports, Ms. Ba had handed him a folder of old clippings and told him to find the moment it started. He had expected something vague, a gradual shift, and instead he had found a date. The first instant replay on television was shown by CBS during the Army-Navy game on December 7, 1963, using a system devised by director Tony Verna. He had written a paragraph about it and moved on, and now here he was, sixty years downstream, sitting in the same rivalry, in a stadium full of people screaming for the technology that man had invented.

"It happened here," Jaxon said. "Not here exactly, but this game. Army-Navy. The first instant replay ever on TV was CBS, December 7, 1963, and the guy who figured out how to do it was a director named Tony Verna."

Hugh turned around again, skeptical. "This game?"

"This matchup. That game." He didn't have all of it straight in his head, and he said so. "I found it for a paper. Before that, if you missed a play, you missed it. It didn't exist twice."

The Navy midshipman behind Hugh had been listening, and now he leaned forward between them, still furious but curious too, the two feelings running side by side. "So before '63 nobody ever saw a play again? That's insane. My whole life is watching plays again."

"Mine too," Jaxon said. And that was the part he couldn't stop turning over, that the fairness Hugh was screaming for was only sixty years old, that for most of the history of this game the crowd had done what the man in the striped shirt said and gone home arguing about it forever. He wasn't sure which was better, honestly. The cameras had made the truth available, but available wasn't the same as delivered, and here they all sat, three giant screens glowing overhead, seeing nothing but a rotating bank logo while the offense lined up.

Army drove to the Navy thirty and missed a field goal, and the game went on the way games go on, absorbing the disputed play into itself. Mekhi argued the fumble to the midshipman through the entire fourth quarter, play by play, and Hugh kept turning around to add evidence, and somewhere in the third argument Jaxon stopped trying to referee the memory of the pile. On the drive home, in the dark of the car, he looked up Tony Verna on his phone, half to check himself, and found the date exactly where he'd left it. He read it twice, then held the screen out to his father at a red light.

"That's the game we were at today," his father said, squinting. "Same two teams."

"Sixty years apart," Jaxon said. "Almost to the day."

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Water boils at a lower temperature at high altitude, about 95 degrees Celsius at 5,000 feet, so boiled foods take longer to cook.
story:
The assignment on the board read "A meal for your family, scaled for four," and Abigail had chosen her grandmother's pasta with brown butter and sage, the dish her mother made on Sundays before the move. She had copied the recipe onto an index card in her grandmother's slanted handwriting, or as close to it as she could manage: boil the pasta eleven minutes, no more. The cooking classroom at her new school smelled like scorched oil and dish soap, and through the windows the peaks stood grey and close, the town tucked against them at five thousand feet.

"You're doing the butter thing again," Esteban said, laying out their station's knives. "It's just pasta, Abigail."

"It's not just pasta. It's eleven minutes. That's the whole recipe. Everything else is feel."

Mylee leaned over from the next burner, where her own sauce was reducing. "I'd trust the feel part over the number part," she said. "Numbers lie when you move."

Ms. Whitaker circled the room with a clipboard, pausing at each station the way a doctor pauses at a bedside. When she reached theirs, she set a small igneous paperweight on the counter, a fist of volcanic glass she carried like a talisman, and watched Abigail slide the pasta into the roiling pot. "Setting a timer?" she asked.

"Eleven minutes. Family recipe."

"Start it," Ms. Whitaker said, and moved on, which Abigail found either encouraging or ominous.

At eleven minutes she lifted a strand, blew on it, and bit. It cracked between her teeth, pale and stiff at the center. She took another strand from the same pot and it was the same, hard where it should have given. "No," she said. "No, this is wrong."

"Your card says eleven," Esteban said. "You followed the card."

"The card was written somewhere else." Abigail stood with the strand in her hand, working it through. Her grandmother had lived her whole life near the coast. The recipe's times belonged to that kitchen, to that elevation, and the numbers had traveled with the paper while the conditions had not. Here the water was different. She had watched it boil and assumed boiling was boiling, a fixed finish line, and now the evidence was in her mouth saying otherwise.

She looked at the pot, still rolling, and thought about what she actually knew. Her mother had complained, their first week in the new house, that everything on the stove took longer than it should, that the potatoes never softened on schedule, and Abigail had assumed her mother was exaggerating, blaming the move for everything the way she blamed the move for the bad reception and the slow mail. But the water here must not get as hot as water at the coast. It boiled, it rolled and hissed and looked exactly the same, but at this altitude it had to be doing its work at a lower temperature, something shy of a hundred degrees. She couldn't say how much. She only knew that cooler water meant slower cooking, and slower cooking meant her grandmother's eleven minutes was a lie in this room even though it had been true in that one.

"So what, you just guess longer?" Esteban asked. He had his phone out. "Fifteen?"

"That's the problem with your whole approach," Mylee said, spoon tapping the rim of her saucepan. "You want to parametrize it. One number in, one time out. Recipes aren't equations."

"They're a little bit equations," Abigail said. "That's what I keep getting wrong. I kept saying it's all feel, like my grandmother, and then the second something broke I treated the number like scripture instead of asking what the number was measuring." She dropped the lid half over the pot and turned the burner up a notch. "The eleven minutes was a measurement of doneness, not a rule. The doneness is still the same. The conditions changed."

Ms. Whitacker drifted back as the clock showed sixteen minutes. Abigail fished out a strand, blew on it, and bit through it clean, the center gone tender, and folded it into the browned butter with the sage crackling against the pan.

At tasting time, Ms. Whitaker announced an amnesty for anyone's first failed attempt, a full credit redo on Thursday, and half the class exhaled. Mylee raised her hand. "Do we get amnesty if we insulted someone's methodology and they turned out to be right?"

"Only if the apology is sincere," Ms. Whitaker said.

Mylee came over and took the second tasting bowl, the one Abigail had filled and pushed across the counter without being asked. She ate standing, then set the bowl down. "Okay. Conditions matter. I was doing the same thing from the other direction." She picked up the index card and turned it over, writing in the margin: at altitude, add time. "What should I put, a number?"

"I don't know the number," Abigail said. "I know it was hard at eleven and done at sixteen, and I know it won't be the same on the coast." She wiped the counter around the igneous paperweight and slid it back toward Ms. Whitaker's end of the station. "Maybe write 'taste at eleven.'"

Esteban was already plating the last of the pasta for the take-home trays, the ones meant to go to their families tonight. He held the container out to her. "Your mom's going to ask why it's late."

Abigail took it, the warmth of it coming through the plastic into her palms. "She'll ask why it's good," she said.

activity: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
knowledge_domain: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
fact: In a minor-key sonata-form movement, the exposition's second theme usually moves to the relative major, such as E-flat major in a movement in C minor.
story:
The church basement smelled of candle wax and old carpet, and Faith had spread her score of Mozart's Piano Sonata in C minor across the folding table normally reserved for coffee hour. Ms. Castillo, who played the organ on Sundays and let students use the sanctuary's old upright on weekday afternoons, had left a jar of coloured pencils beside the hymnal shelf, and Faith had claimed them all: blue for the first theme, green for the second, red for the development. Her analysis was due Friday, and she had put it off long enough that postponement had begun to feel like a moral failing rather than a scheduling problem.

Jawad arrived twenty minutes late with two cans of soda and no apology, which was his way. He dropped into the chair across from her, cracked his can, and leaned over the score with the wariness of someone inspecting a legal document he suspected he had signed. "You're still on the exposition," he said. "We were supposed to finish this last week."

"I was finishing other things last week." She had been, too: her mother's extra shifts, her brother's rides to practice, a litany of obligations that Faith privately suspected she used, sometimes, as armor against harder work. She was not proud of the suspicion, and she had not shared it with anyone, not even Alena, who would have understood it immediately and said so in fewer words than Faith could bear.

She set the needle on the portable turntable Ms. Castillo kept beside the piano, and the first theme came through the basement's bad acoustics with all its C minor gravity intact. Faith marked the bar with blue. Then, at the transition, she did what she had done in her notebook at home: she drew a green bracket several bars early, listening for the second theme to arrive in the dominant, in G minor, the way her textbook said minor-key themes pushed toward.

"You put the green in the wrong place," Jawad said, and she told him to wait, and then the second theme arrived, and it was not what either of them expected. It was bright. It was unmistakably major, and the E-flat arpeggios unspooled under her pencil hand with a warmth that seemed to interpose itself between the listener and the storm of the opening, like sunlight through a doorway in a wall she had assumed was solid.

"That's not G," Jawad said. "Is that E-flat?"

"Three flats," Faith said, counting the signature with her finger, her voice going flat with the peculiar embarrassment of being wrong in front of someone. She erased the bracket. In a movement in C minor, she wrote in the margin, the second theme moves to E-flat major, the relative major, and sat looking at the sentence as though it were a confession. Somewhere in her binder there was a note from class, she was almost sure, that she had copied without reading.

Alena came down the stairs with her backpack still on, having found the side door unlocked as Faith knew she would. "Ms. Castillo says if you touch the organ she'll make you sing the offertory alone," she announced, and then she saw their faces and pulled up a chair. Faith played the second theme again, and Alena, who was the real pianist of the three and an unrepentant epicure about recordings, closed her eyes through the phrase. "E-flat," she said, before the last chord had settled. "The relative major. It's like the movement steps outside itself for a minute."

"It's modulating to the dominant," Jawad said, with the certainty he reserved for things he had half learned, and Faith shook her head and pushed the score across the table so he could see the key signature and the margin note in her own hand. He was quiet for a moment, the way he was when a fact rearranged something he had been confident about, and then he marked the bracket himself, in the right place, in green, without being asked.

They worked until the light through the basement windows went from white to amber. The development section turned out to be easier to find than either of them had feared; it announced itself by taking the themes apart, and the recapitulation brought the second theme back home to C minor, darkened, no longer borrowed light. Faith drew the red pencil through the development in one long stroke and thought, not for the first time, that the form was an argument: something stated, something challenged, something restated with the challenge absorbed into it. Whether that was what Mozart intended, or only what her Friday deadline needed him to have intended, she could not decide, and she left the question in the margin beside the note, unresolved, where it seemed to belong.

When the others had packed up and gone, she stayed to put the pencils back in the jar. Ms. Castillo passed through on her way to lock the sanctuary, paused at the table, and looked at the score for a moment with its blue and green and red. She said nothing about the analysis, only, "Turn the lights off when you go," and her footsteps went up the stairs. Faith stood a little longer in the half dark with her hand on the piano's closed lid, then opened it and played the second theme one more time, the E-flat arpeggios rising into the empty room.
